speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the very positive approach taken by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). I hope throughout the day there will be a useful exchange and that all of us will contribute as we can to see how we can improve the tourist industry in this country.
I welcome the fact that the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) has raised this as an issue. It gives us an opportunity to debate what I consider, and I know he considers, to be a very important industry in this country. I know of his concern for and interest in the industry and his desire to see it improved. I do not want to be partisan, except I must make some clarification. As a Prince Edward Islander, I know the Hon. Member will forgive me. He knows how Maritimers debate.
I will not deal with everything the Hon. Member said. I do, however, want to deal with the Prince Edward Island portion of his speech. While the Hon. Member's motion states that the Government of Canada neglects the Canadian tourist industry, I am sure the Hon. Member will agree that it can hardly be said that it neglects Prince Edward Island, where we are involved in a comprehensive development plan costing $15 million over 15 years, 90 per cent of which is federal.
There is a $39 million federal development strategy in P.E.I. In addition, there is a $3.8 million contribution to a convention centre-hotel complex in Charlottetown. As we know, the developers had some financial difficulty. The Government of Canada is co-operating with the Government of P.E.I. and the developers and has said it will guarantee a $19 million bank loan to ensure that this convention centre-hotel complex goes ahead. That is $15 million, $39 million, $3.8 million and a $19 million loan guarantee. While the charge is made that there has been neglect, I do not think that is neglect.
There was also an indication that somehow unilateral delivery was not well received. I should like to read from an article which appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian on February 1, 1982, by Roseanne McCabe. She writes:
You'll not find many Island tourist operators knocking the federal government's recent dollar transfusion into the tourism industry.
"It's a first as far as major dollars going directly to help the operators," Don Groom, president of the P.E.I. Tourism Industry Association, says of the $5.4 million tourism development program announced last week.
Island politicians say the federal government stole their thunder ... but the operators don't seem to mind.
"I'm relieved to see the federal government funding the program," says Steve Bezanson, operator of Rustico Summer Haven.
Later she goes on to say:
Mr. Groom says the program is a "real break" for the industry. One in four persons works in tourism during the summer.
There is evidence from the people involved in the industry that they welcome these funds and the involvement of the Government of Canada in tourism in Prince Edward Island which is so important to that Province. Perhaps of all Provinces it is the one most involved in tourism and we want to see that continue.
Next year marks the 50th anniversary of active involvement of the Government of Canada in the marketing and development of tourism in this country. We began with a staff of three and an annual budget of $100,000 in 1934. That has grown into what we know as the Canadian Government Office of Tourism, or what I like to call "Tourism Canada". I do not know how Hon. Members feel about that but it seems to me to sum up the things we want to say about tourism in Canada. It is Canadian, it operates all across the country and it is unified. It has a ring to it. I put it to Hon. Members that with their support we might be able to call it "Tourism Canada" and one of these days we might even go a little further. I will not say anything more about that at the present time.
I will.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) will have more to say about that.
The CGOT uses the most sophisticated marketing development tools available and has an annual budget of $42 million. It attracts more than 40 million people per year to Canada. The Government knows that the tourism sector of the country is important. It is a sector that is largely Canadian owned and is operated for the most part by small businessmen. There are
100,000	businesses across the country-mostly small businesses-involved in the industry.
Every year it brings $16.5 billion into the country or 5 per cent of our Gross National Product. It means $28 billion income for Canadians and one million Canadians are employed in the industry. In 1981 it brought in $7.5 billion in Government revenues. If I were in my former portfolio I would be saying how great it is to have that tax money coming in. It brings in $2.5 billion in investments and $3.8 billion in foreign exchange. It is a prime way of acquiring foreign exchange. Tourism is big business and the Government is aware of that, but the country has been beset by economic difficulties. Despite that, however, the tourism industry has maintained its relative position within the overall economy and has performed
April 14, 1983

better than a lot of other industries. The growth and travel expenditure almost equals the rate of inflation. That can be matched by few other industrial sector. For a quick fix in the economy, we do not have to look beyond tourism in which a small amount of money can create a lot of jobs. Tourism outperformed forestry, manufacturing, construction and trade in levels of employment between 1979 and 1981.
That is what we have to say today to the unconverted. I assume that those Members who are in the House are here to preach the message. As the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain said, we want to send a message from all sides of the House to people in Canada who do not understand that the tourism industry is important and can perform a service for the country. It ranks first, second or third as an industry in every Province of Canada. Tourism employs women, young people, native people and unskilled people. The CGOT has more than 40 federal Departments and agencies that support the tourism industry through, for instance, Parks Canada, fisheries, the Department of the Secretary of State and others.
We should not forget the contribution of the Federal Business Development Bank. By volume and value, 23 per cent of the bank's lending flows into the tourism and recreation sector, so it is a very important supporter of the industry.
It is precisely because of the importance that the Government attaches to employment and economic growth that it has assigned a priority to tourism. The federal Government is telling Canadians, as we are doing today, about the importance of the industry.
Just recently I published a pamphlet which I hope Hon. Members will help to distribute. I know that visual aids are not allowed in the House but there it is. It says "Tourism is Big Business". More than one million jobs depend on it. I am borrowing this technique from my friends across the way, Mr. Speaker. This pamphlet has been distributed and I hope Hon. Members will help with wider distribution as we want Canadians to understand how important tourism is to them.
In the months that I have occupied this portfolio I have travelled from one end of Canada to the other. The Hon. Member for Malpeque knows that as he and I were together in Vancouver. I have been to the Northwest Territories and Yukon and before the end of June I will be back there. I have not been to Prince Edward Island yet but I am going. I think it is important that we tell the story all across the country.
Shortly after my appointment I spoke to the National Tour Association in Toronto. I was pleased when a number of American delegates said that they regard Canada as a great destination and were sending hundreds of thousands of Americans here year round. They spend $90 million per year. At that same convention, for the first time ever a Canadian was named the travel leader of the year. I was very proud that he was an official of the Canadian Government Office of Tourism.
The Prime Minister!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Many Hon. Members are aware that we are in the process of creating the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion from the Department of Industry, Trade and
Supply
Commerce and DREE. I can tell the House that tourism is a priority of that Department. We have reviewed operational plans and I am pleased to inform the House that the proposed regional tourism initiatives will represent a significant increase in federal spending on tourism development and marketing over the next five years.
As Hon. Members will know, the reorganization provides that federal tourism marketing operations abroad become the responsibility of the Department of External Affairs. This means that effectively we have more horsepower. We have more horsepower overseas, and as a result of the reorganization of DRIE we are going to have more delivery agents all across the country in a decentralized way. I was in Vancouver recently talking to the DRIE people there is our office, and I can say that all across the country we have strong regional centres which are able to deliver our programs.
As a result of reorganization we, in tourism, are going to have more delivery agents, not less, across this country. We will have more trade commissioners in other parts of the world also. This increases Canada's marketing presence from 21 posts to over 100 posts overseas which are administered by the Department of External Affairs. I was overseas recently in West Berlin, and while I was there, apart from visiting the International Tourist Bourse, I addressed 18 of our trade commissioners who had been assigned tourism responsibilities in various countries. There is a real market overseas. There is a market in West Germany, in Switzerland and in Italy. Our foreign visitors are increasing. In my talk I impressed upon these 18 trade commissioners the importance of tourism and the fact that they had to get out and sell the product on our behalf. I believe they will respond and I will be doing a followup with them.
On that same trip I opened the Canadian exhibit at the International Tourism Bourse. The Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) was with me and was helping to promote Canadian wine, among other things. The International Tourism Bourse is the largest event of its kind in the world. The federal Government brought together some 55 Canadian participants in one place in a co-operative effort to promote travel to Canada. I want to stress as well that the reorganization has resulted in a doubling of the numbers of federal tourism specialists stationed across Canada.
Our real thrust will be next year, 1984. I believe it should be regarded as "The year of tourism in Canada". The year 1984 will be the 450th anniversary of the arrival of Jacques Cartier in Canada, to begin with-the birth of Canada, if you like. These observances will have meaning for all Canadians, not just Quebec. It is a significant Canadian event. The year 1984 will also be the bicentenary of New Brunswick as a Province. It will be the bicentenary of the Loyalist settlement in Ontario.
All these events all across the country will have a spin-off for tourism and we should take advantage of them. We should make a real effort in 1984 to promote tourism. We are gearing

April 14, 1983
Supply
up for that already. I can tell Hon. Members that the Government of Canada has put together some special teams in order to make sure of that.
1 would like to pay tribute to my colleague, the former Minister responsible for tourism, the Hon. Charles Lapointe. He did a great job for tourism, and I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that his involvement has not stopped. He is very active in putting together and promoting this 450th anniversary celebration, and so are other Ministers. We are trying to produce a comprehensive package which will really emphasize what is happening in this country in 1984.
As I mentioned earlier, 1984 will mark the 50th anniversary of federal Government co-operation and collaboration with the Provinces and Territories. I believe we should make it a launching pad for a new initiative in tourism because I want to see tourism get a higher profile in Government circles. I intend to impress upon my Cabinet colleagues the economic and social impact of tourism and point out to them the relevance to tourism of their policies and operations.
I believe, considering existing resource levels, that the tourism program of the federal Government has been demonstrated to be a very cost-effective one. There are, however, factors working against our getting the job done, and we might as well recognize that. One prime example is that the advertising budget, due to inflation and uncontrollable cost increases, has eroded over the last ten years. This has occurred in the face of worldwide competition. For example, Governments in the United States spent nearly $200 million on advertising and promotion last year. It was reported in yesterday's The Globe and Mail that British Airways plans to spend $50 million on travel advertising in Canada, all of it to encourage people to travel out of Canada. We know that there are more than 50 foreign national tourism organizations in Canada, plus some 75 foreign airlines, which are all singing the siren song of faraway places outside of Canada. There are people in Canada who are trying to get people to travel to other countries. It is the old story. Therefore we must make sure that as many as possible of our resources are used to keep Canadians travelling in Canada. That is where the great advantage is. That is where the bulk of our money is going to come from, from Canadians as well as people from the United States travelling in Canada. There is an increasing number of tourists from Europe, but the main thrust has to be in this country, first of all, and then the United States.
I can tell the House that I am certainly going to go after more funds for the federal marketing of tourism. Then I am going to press forward with regional initiatives, as we have in the past, to improve the resources and facilities we have in a marketing effort right across this country. I want to establish a tourism industry advisory council. I want to talk to the people, the entrepreneurs, in the industry. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain made the point that Governments cannot do it all alone. We must talk to the people who work in the industry and to the people who operate within the industry. I want to tell him I intend to set up that advisory board and I am going to listen to it. I hope that we will have business and
labour on that board. The future of tourism requires collective effort. It requires collaboration and co-operation and, for my part, I want to see that come about.
We are coming out of a tough time in this country when Canada has not been everything that we wanted it to be, and we have had problems all over the world. But one thing that tourism can do, apart from creating jobs and making money, perhaps as well as or better than any other Government Department, is to tell Canadians about Canada, what this country is like, what it means and how proud they should be to be citizens of Canada. Tourism can have a monumental effect on Canadian unity. That is one reason we should all be behind the program. It goes beyond dollars and cents. It brings Canadians together and it can bring Canada together. I know that all my colleagues in the House will support the efforts we make in the future to make sure that Canadians know the importance of this industry for making money, for job creation, but, most important of all, for the promotion of national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I am very encouraged by the Minister's remarks that he for one, on the Government side of the House, appreciates the value of tourism. He made a speech in Vancouver and said that the Government of Canada recognizes the importance of this industry. Well, I have some doubts about that. He went on to say: "If I had my way, the Government would do more". I was there when he delivered that speech. I believe he was sincere. I hope that he will follow through on his commitment that, as Minister responsible for tourism, he will do more.
In the speech he made in Vancouver he said: "I propose to establish a caucus committee on tourism to harness the interest that is regularly voiced by individual Members of Parliament. In time such an institution might largely evolve into a standing committee of the House of Commons". My first question, Mr. Speaker, is: What is happening with that commitment to the association? Has the Minister taken steps to initiate a standing committee on tourism?
Secondly, in his speech the Minister said: "I intend to examine your association's conviction", meaning TIAC, "and urge that tourism within the federal Government be a separate ministry". I would like his answers to those two questions, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
With regard to the first question, I think the start should be made not only in caucus but the caucuses. I would like to have the caucuses on both sides of the House come and sit down with us in the Canadian Government Office of Tourism. I make that offer now. I know the Hon. Member's interest; I have talked with certain Members of the NDP about this and with certain Members on this side of the House, including our chairman of the national caucus. My staff is now in the process of setting up a timetable whereby all caucuses can visit with us. We can tell them what we have on our minds
April 14, 1983

and get some input from them as to how they think that should be modified, changed or proceeded with.
With regard to the standing committee, I think that will be something we can examine and look forward to. But I think the first step should be to get caucus input, and I can assure the Hon. Member that that is being worked on very actively.
With regard to the other suggestion from T1AC that there should be a separate ministry, I can tell the Hon. Member that from my point of view it will get very serious consideration. If we are serious about what we are saying today concerning the importance of this industry, we must use all possible vehicles to focus on it and promote it.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister not only has responsibility for tourism but for small business as well. I would like him to indicate what assistance is provided to small tourist businesses in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
As I said in my speech, Mr. Speaker, 23 per cent of loans by the FBDB have been for tourism purposes. Within our own Department we have a program which can make available up to $25,000, or 50 per cent of the effort involved in putting together tour packages, market research, promotion brochures and that kind of thing. We do have that kind of program which can be delivered directly to entrepreneurs in the tourism industry. Of course, there is a whole range of small business programs available to tourist operators. With the co-operation of the Opposition we recently passed an extension to the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Small Business Investment Grants Act, and those mechanisms are available to the people in the industry.
More than anything, I guess, we have had an effect on small business through the development agreements with the Provinces all across the country. In that way there has been direct lending and direct grants to motel and tour operators and people with tourist facilities. So there has been a very active program of assistance to small business. We know that most of the businesses in tourism are small businesses and we have to keep them happy and healthy.

Mr. Speaker, what tends to happen a lot in the tourist industry is that we see support and promotion for the already established areas in the southern part of the country. Can we expect any kind of emphasis or support from the Minister for tourism in the north or less developed areas?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
I am very glad the Hon. Member raised that question because I happen to represent the north. I know the potential and how important tourism can be to the north. I can tell him, as I said earlier in my speech, that 1 have already been to the Northwest Territories and Yukon. However, I have been invited to both places again. We do have now a very active agreement with the Northwest Territories and we have been discussing an agreement with the Yukon. I met Mr. Pearson from the Yukon when he was here a little while ago. I very much want to see an emphasis in those areas.
Supply
When I was in Yukon there were a lot of German tourists canoeing in the Yukon. There is a fair amount of direct involvement by German tourists in the Yukon. So not only Canadians but a lot of Europeans are going directly into the north because they want that wilderness experience. I can tell him that I am aware of it, I am all for it and I am going to see that it is promoted and enhanced.

Mr. Speaker, the specific concern I have relates to Wood Buffalo National Park. As the Minister is likely aware, there has been conditional approval for a road through the park which would contribute a great deal to tourism in the Territories and in Whitehorse, but also in the northern part of Alberta. The difficulty is that no Government department is prepared to put any funding in place for the development of a road in that area to open it up to tourism. Can we expect some help from the Minister in that particular regard?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
I would certainly take a look at that situation to see what we could do. National parks, as he knows, is under a different Ministry.
I might take this time to emphasize the importance to tourism of those national parks. I said earlier that a great many Government departments have an impact on tourism. All the marinas, for example, created under the Small Craft Harbours Branch of the Department of Fisheries have been so important for tourism. Indeed, we have a special program in Quebec related to the celebrations next year, and a series of marinas that we hope will not only focus on the importance of the historical significance of the St. Lawrence River to Canada but, indeed, encourage tourists to go there.
As to national parks, I can name them all across the country. In my own Province, we have Gros Morne where the expenditures we made were so important to attracting tourists. I do not know all the details of the specific case the Hon. Member has raised, but I can tell him that I am quite prepared to discuss it with my colleagues and to be of any help we can be in focusing on that problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure to take part in this Opposition day. I have been in this House for ten and a half years and seen Opposition days on wheat, fish and sundry other items. Perhaps my memory is not too good, but I believe this is the first one on tourism.
I assume that tourism is not a really big business; it is merely $16.5 billion. That is peanuts, I suppose. In other words, I am being slightly facetious, because if any industry is prominent and of great importance to this great Dominion of Canada, it is the tourist industry.
That brings up the position of the Hon. Minister as Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism. I take exception to that title because, first of all, he should not be a Minister of State; that is a very high profile Department and, with all due respect to the illustrious Postmaster General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), the Minister

April 14, 1983
Supply
sitting behind him is bringing in money to pay for his Department as well as a great many other Departments. We call it CGOT. I do not like that; it does not sound impressive enough. The Minister's own idea, Tourism Canada, to me, is very important. I think that matter should come up before his caucus next Wednesday and be endorsed unanimously as Tourism Canada. That is easier to sell than the Canadian Government Office of Tourism. I am quite sure that Members on the Government bench will agree with that. This is a very important Department, a big money-maker, and it can be a much bigger money-maker in the years to come.
The Minister pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that $16.5 billion is 5 per cent of the GNP. Well, let us see some of these other Department heads get up and tell us what they are collecting or putting into the coffers. I am quite sure it will not be near that amount.
The other important thing he mentioned was the generation of foreign exchange, I think he said $3.8 billion. That is a lot of money coming in, especially offshore money.
The Minister also mentioned the Department of Regional Industry Expansion, known as DRIE. I do not know whether I like DRIE as well as DREE because I am afraid you are going to dry up the funds. I am aware that DREE has done a great job in promoting tourism in the Atlantic area, but when it comes to Ontario it has been pretty hard to get any money out of DREE. I believe that $4 million was allocated for the entire Province of Ontario under a DREE provincial co-operative deal. Let us hope that that amount will be increased a great deal more.
I was also pleased to hear the Minister mention the small craft harbours and how important they are. In the Province of Ontario there are 450 small craft harbours. It is pretty difficult, when we approach the officials in Burlington, to get money. They are most co-operative, but they say: "Well, yes, we know that it is important, but word has come down from on high that there will not be money available". Years ago it had even been reduced, and in the great Province of Ontario, which has more tourists than every other Province put together, the total amount for small craft harbours was somewhere in the area of $3 million to $4 million.
However, the Government can pump $30 million or $40 million into one particular harbour. I am thinking of the harbours at Montreal, Halifax, and probably those out west. Those are certainly important, but let us get down to basics and consider where we can get the biggest bang for the bucks. I am quite sure that it is in those small harbours, because an awful lot of boats are tying up there and much gasoline is being sold there, of which rumour has it that the federal Government takes a pretty healthy cut.
In questioning the Minister one Hon. Member mentioned the fact that the Minister was the Minister responsible for small business as well as tourism. To me, small business and
tourism are pretty well synonymous, because most of the tourist operators are small businessmen.
It is also important to remember that in this time of high unemployment a great many of the unemployed, I believe over half, have been laid off by small business industries and individual entrepreneurs who have not been able to continue to grow and prosper, who have had to cut down, and who, in many cases, have just closed up their doors and said they could not continue any longer. Then, of course, a staggering amount of them have actually declared bankruptcy. That is certainly very important to consider, in my view. It is why the Government must give a much higher profile to the tourist industry and should also see that money is provided in special ways, at least with long-term, low interest rates, and guaranteed interest rates. This should be done now rather than in a year or two.
Many tourist operators came to me last summer and fall with tears in their eyes. They were faced with having to renew mortgages. Sure, they could gamble. However, they had to renew for five years at 17 per cent or 18 per cent when their mortgages were probably in the 10 per cent or 11 per cent bracket before. It made the difference as to whether they would be able to keep their doors open.
I know that money is scarce. I am well aware of the staggering deficit with which the country is faced. Tuesday night will be the night when we will see what will happen. I hope that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism has been able to have a word with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his officials to see that something is done to help the tourist industry, because that is all-important.
I consider the fact that the Government can most blissfully find money for some other projects. Some of them have been given quite a bit of money, such as $500 million to bail out Dome Petroleum. Would it not be nice to give that amount to the tourist operators across Canada? Speaking of Dome Petroleum, $2.6 million will be given as a golden handshake to Mr. Gallagher when he turns over the reins of Dome Petroleum in September. The sum of $2.6 million would certainly help a good number of tourist operators to improve or possibly save their businesses. The sum of $1.4 billion was given for the takeover of Petrofina, with $600 million given to BP Canada to take over just the unproductive part of that particular firm. Then in the newpapers yesterday we heard about Canadair, another Crown-owned company. The Hon. Member shrugs his shoulders. We do not know just how serious it will be. The Government can find money for all these massive projects, but when it comes to the little, individual businessman, the tourist entrepreneur, the money is just not there.
If one goes to the Federal Business Development Bank, yes, it will provide money but the rates are certainly scary to a great many. Innumerable tourist operators have gone there and have then gone to ordinary banking or trust institutions and done better. I will admit that the FBDB is sort of a lender of last resort. However, when the Government can loan money
April 14, 1983

out at very advantageous rates to some of these huge multinationals, surely it could do the same or more for some of these small businesses, these tourist operators across the country who will probably be providing a great many more jobs per dollar loaned than those massive ones are providing.
The tourist industry is certainly one of the most important ones. Because of its nature, it is widely spread over the entire country, perhaps more than most other industries. That would possibly include agriculture as well. It is rooted in the rural areas of the nation: Parry Sound-Muskoka, out west, Newfoundland, Labrador, the Minister's own backyard. For that reason, it seems to me that if the Government really wants to trigger a widespread recovery in our country, this is the place to start. I do not think we have done nearly as well as we should have in this area.
Conversely, there are a number of things we could do which would make a real difference. Let us consider a few statistics for a start. First, we know that over the past few years we in Canada have been running a deficit on our tourist account with the United States alone of $1 billion a year. That means that Canadians are spending $1 billion more every year than Americans are spending here. That does not take into consideration all the millions of dollars spent in Europe and elsewhere. In 1981, for example, Canadians spent $3.5 billion in the United States while visiting Americans left $2.5 billion here. That is a shocking spread which does not need to be so. Such was not the case before. In fact, the spread was always in Canada's favour.
Let us bear in mind just how big in industry it is that we are discussing. We all admit that last year was not a good year, but Ontario alone saw revenues of $7.4 billion which generated a ripple effect throughout the economy in Ontario of some $12.6 billion. That is big bucks any way one looks at it.
What, then, could we do to improve the situation for this very key industry? There are a number of things which I have been pressing personally, as has been my Party. Of course, I re-emphasize that there should be higher priority and profile given to the Ministry. There should be a Minister of Tourism per se, not a Minister of State for Tourism.
Let us next discuss taxes. Every dollar which is left behind by a tourist in the form of profit to an operator generates income tax and taxes for various other Governments. Businessmen are familiar with the idea of spending a dollar to make a dollar. Perhaps Governments should think about doing the same. In their case, of course, spending a dollar would mean cutting the taxes a bit so as to encourage more tourism.
The Minister stated that the advertising budget for tourism had been cut. While money can be saved by cutting down on advertising, the end result will be a greater deficit. It is necessary to advertise because it pays to advertise. The product must be sold. I have heard it said: "You do not sell the steak, you sell the sizzle." We need advertisements that will induce people to come to this wonderful country of Canada. Once they come here they have to be encouraged to come to the
Supply
fabulous tourist area of Parry Sound-Muskoka. I assume that Prince Edward Island also has many attractions, as does Newfoundland and Labrador.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: I have been to Parry Sound-Muskoka.

The Minister should certainly be speaking strongly about the money he needs to advertise this great country. This should be done through Tourism Canada, not that CGOT. Let us hope that will end before too long.
The Government is certainly well known for its advertising, as has been suggested to the Government from this side time and again. It squanders literally millions of dollars on advertising its own programs. But we are speaking of advertising Canada which will bring money back into the country fourfold. If advertising was not valuable, why do the automobile companies still spend millions of dollars on advertising even though they are feeling the pinch? The soap companies know the importance of advertising. Therefore I hope Members of Parliament recognize that advertising is extremely important in order to sell Canada and bring tourists here.
A factor which disturbs tourists, Canadians as well as others, is the cost of a holiday in Canada. A major cost of that holiday is the price of gasoline. That is the real horror story. By the time the Provinces and the federal Government take their share, gas is quite costly. With all due respect to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, a gallon of gasoline - I did not say litre - costs almost twice as much here as in the United States.
This raises another point. Many American tourists who visit Canada are not enamoured of the metric mess which is occurring. The Minister may smile even slightly but he knows that that is bloody well right. Do not shake your head that way, shake it the other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: I am much more tolerant than you.

You are the intolerant one. I am tolerant. I am willing to accept metric on a voluntary basis but I am not willing, nor are many other Canadians, to have it shoved down our throats under the threat of "You do this or you go to jail". You have not put that guy Halpert in jail or the Members out at Carleton Place because this is still a reasonably free country.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: They are coming here because they are seeing something different. They do not want to be in America.

They are seeing something different all right, and expensively too.
In any event something must be done to attract tourists to our country. As has been mentioned here, the Minister has been told how tourists will be attracted to our respective regions. I am aware of the fact that the Government agency, Tourism Canada, has the job of bringing people to the borders of Canada. It is then up to the Provinces to entice those people to their respective regions.
I hope that there will be 100 per cent co-operation between the various provincial offices of tourism and Tourism Canada

April 14, 1983
Supply
to prevent any overlap and allow money to be distributed and spent more efficiently. This co-operation would allow the federal Government through Tourism Canada to do a much better job. Tourism Canada is a very important agency. This industry is one of the best money-makers that exists. It is not necessary to build million dollar plants to generate taxes, and that is an important consideration.
Another issue I wish to raise, which indirectly concerns tourism but has a great effect upon it, is acid rain. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) at this moment is hosting a lunch for the Subcommittee on Acid Rain. I am well aware that the Government recognizes the seriousness of the acid rain problem and that the Minister of the Environment is doing his very best to convey that message to our neighbours in the United States. If we do not address this problem in a meaningful way, our tourist industry will suffer because acid rain is already having an adverse affect on many of our lakes. I am certain the fish population in those lakes is being depleted, and while the mature fish may not be affected by acid rain, serious problems will occur during spawning and the growth of young fish in the years to come.
Once again, the funds needed to address this problem will be hard to get from the Minister of Finance or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) in these times but there are certain matters which are very important. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) will be able to do a selling job on the Secretary of State in the United States. He was certainly not too optimistic yesterday in answering questions from our critic, the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan). The Secretary of State for External Affairs is adept at not saying anything while talking a great deal, but he did not say anything too promising.
I want to emphasize once again for the Minister just how important the acid rain problem will be to the tourist industry through the years. We have heard statistics on the thousands of lakes that have been damaged by acid rain. Some say there are 4,000 lakes in Ontario that are in a pretty serious situation, but there are 140,000 lakes. We are among those most blessed with the facilities for tourists, including Canadians, Americans and others from offshore. It is up to us and the Minister through his department to try to attract as many of these offshore and American tourists as possible. I know that they want the most for their money.
I close by saying that we must put more emphasis on the attraction of European tourists. German tourists are coming here in greater numbers each year and they are the ones who have the money. They are the ones we want to see here.
I hope next Tuesday's budget will provide some relief for the tourist operators so that they can improve their facilities and get money for working capital. I know it is difficult to get money when one goes to a hard-nosed bank which will only lend money based on one's assets. Yet Massey-Ferguson and other companies like it can borrow with assets which do not meet what the Government shells out for them.
I want to commend the Minister for the job he is doing. I am aware that he is having difficulty with his own Cabinet colleagues but he should speak that much louder and get the support of his backbenchers. Perhaps the Treasury benches will stop and listen to how important his department is. Once again, I say that he should be the Minister of Tourism and nothing else.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions, comments and answers?
Before I recognize the next Hon. Member in debate, it would be appropriate if I now look to my right. However, the Chair was advised that one Hon. Member has a travel problem. I have heard nothing since then. Unless I hear something now, I will look to my right.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the comments of the Hon. Member with great interest. I was also very impressed by the comments made by the Minister responsible for Tourism Canada. I think we should remember that in addition to the financial aspects there are also cultural and technical factors to be considered. It is very easy to make speeches in the House and try to prove that the Government has failed to support tourism in Canada, but if we take a closer look at the facts, it becomes clear that the Canadian Government is doing a lot to develop an industry that, at first, was relatively marginal.
A good example, Mr. Speaker, is that in Quebec, the tourist industry comes first, even before the pulp and paper industry. This proves more clearly than anything else that both in Canada and in the provinces individually, tourism is recognized as one of the prime factors of development at both the provincial and the federal level.
Before I go any further, Mr. Speaker, I think it should be pointed out that Canadians themselves must be willing to become tourists in their own country. It is all very well to emphasize advertising abroad to encourage people from other countries to visit ours, but it is also very important for Canadians from all parts of this country to visit each other and learn to know their own country.
One of the basic elements of tourism is novelty. We like to exchange our own environment for something new, to experience contrast, enjoy a change of scene and see other people instead of always seeing people we know. As a country, Canada is able to provide that change of scene within its borders, and we can enjoy our differences while understanding what holds us together. I thought it was very interesting to hear the comments of the Hon. Member on Newfoundland, Canada's North and Labrador. I think that as a result of its diversity, Canada provides an incredible range of scenery and impressions. I think there are very few other countries that have so much worth seeing within their own borders. As far as
April 14, 1983

the tourism industry is concerned, we have a federal agency supporting federal initiatives, and we have ten provinces, each with their own tourist offices. Some provinces even have Departments of Tourism, and all this adds up to a formidable instrument for developing the industry. In addition, there are many joint efforts being made by the Canadian Government with the provinces and the municipalities. In fact, the contribution of the latter is often overlooked.
When I was listening to the Hon. Member just now, he was wondering what the Federal Government was doing to demonstrate the vitality of the tourist industry. There are a number of brochures, and I have one here, that describe quite admirably the various regions of our country. This is a brochure that is distributed in Canada for Canadians, and there are others that are distributed in Europe and in other parts of the world such as Japan and which describe the attractions of tourism in Canada.
It would have been interesting to hear just now how many foreigners actually visit this country. Figures are always interesting. In fact, in 1982, 32.5 million Americans came to Canada. They crossed the border to visit Canada, on trips of varying duration, but the fact remains that more than 32 million people did so. That is more than the total population of Canada. I think that on both sides of the House Members will agree that if 32 million Americans came to Canada, that is primarily because there are adequate transportation facilities, the right infrastructures and finally, the right tourism facilities to make it possible for them to stay here. I feel that is important. Of course, the number of tourists may fluctuate from year to year, and the recession in this part of the world may also affect this number, but on average, these figures reflect the number of Americans visiting our country.
We had 474,097 visitors from the United Kingdom, 219,000 from West Germany, 139,000 from Japan, 132,000 from France, 79,000 from The Netherlands, 67,000 from Australia,
62,000	from Italy, 48,000 from Switzerland, 44,000 from Mexico, 44,000 from Israel, 39,000 from Hong Kong, 24,000 from Sweden and 19,000 from Belgium. I am mentioning these figures to show that we already have a substantial number of people, other than Canadians and Americans, who visit our country.
At this stage, we should find out whether our Canadian representatives abroad and our commercially oriented Departments are doing everything they can in this respect and whether more can be done to increase the number of tourists visiting our country. That is a very important point. I think that criticizing and saying that nothing is being done is of no help at all in the debate on this question. It would have been far more interesting to hear some concrete proposals from the Hon. Member on the other side of the House. We must not forget that there have been many Canadian events, subsidized by the Federal and Provincial Governments, which have attracted people from other countries to Canada, for instance,
Supply
Expo 67 in Montreal and the Olympic Games in 1976, the Calgary Games, the Commonwealth Games, and in fact, Vancouver will soon be hosting a world event Transport 1986. These are events that attract tourists from all over the world to our country, but when we ask the support of the House in preparing for these events, that support is not always unanimous. Many Members of the Opposite side of the House object from time to time to these events, while they should in fact be supporting them, because it is this kind of events that will make our country better known. It is a fact that people who come to visit these events return to their own country with a better knowledge of what we have to offer.
Mr. Speaker, there are some very well designed and very well written brochures distributed world-wide that provide a host of details on our country. And for the information of Members on both sides of the House who have had occasion to travel throughout the world, I would like to add that in all airports and cities they will find quite substantial documentation on what Canada has to offer in the way of tourism.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point I would like to raise and that is, that the provinces should work together with the Federal Government to maximize the benefits of tourism for our country. The contribution of Parks Canada was not singled out earlier. If tourism was able to develop as quickly as it did in Western Canada, it is perhaps due to Parks Canada and the major impact of Jasper and Banff, and it is because of the railroads that tourists have been better able to appreciate the West and the Rockies. Then, there is Newfoundland, and 1 believe that the Hon. Minister responsible for Tourism Canada is very familiar with this issue. When we look at the extraordinary Bonavista Park on Bonavista Bay in Newfoundland, we can see what the Federal Government has accomplished with the cooperation of the province of Newfoundland. I think that Canadians have many wonderful things to discover in that region.
The same is true in Ontario, where Parks Canada and the federal government in designating and developing natural areas for all Canadians to visit so that future generations may continue to develop them while maintaining their touristic and natural potential. In Quebec, we have real touristic jewels in the Forillon and St. Maurice Parks. However it is unfortunate that Quebec is reluctant to participate in other such developments because more and more Canadians appreciate the great outdoors. While 60 per cent of Canadians used to live in rural areas, the trend has reversed in the last 15 or 20 years; two thirds of Canadians now live in cities and only one third in the country. Urban residents increasingly want to find recreation outside the cities, and in this regard, I believe that the development program of Parks Canada is one of the major elements of tourism development in Canada.

April 14, 1983
Supply
It is a fact that if Quebec participated more in the development of other Canadian parks on its territory, more Canadians from other provinces would visit Quebec, just as many Quebecers now go elsewhere in Canada to visit other parks. All these elements together promote tourism development in Canada. As I said earlier, it is a matter of attitude. It might not be essential to spend more money for Tourism Canada, even though it is important to have enough money to meet our various needs, but it is really important to change the urge people have to travel outside the country. It is important to change this attitude because we have too great a tendency to go outside Canada for our holidays when, with a little effort, we could perhaps benefit from what our own country and the various provinces and municipalities can offer us throughout the year. In this regard, the Canadian Government has published a brochure called Events 83. This publication lists the events which are held in various municipalities, as well as the dates of these events and a summary of activities.
So, something is being done. Perhaps Tourism Canada could be criticized for not being close enough to the people. Its brochures are kept in offices which might be somewhat overspecialized. Tourism Canada could perhaps provide more information to Canadians so that they might examine what is available, make their decision and visit their own country more easily. It is a fact that other governments, other countries, travel agencies and even transport companies in their advertising are using an approach which is closer to the people than our own government. I suggest that we should up-date our marketing methods and bring tourist information into the homes of Canadians in order to convince them to change their attitude.
Time permitting, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal now with regional tourist offices. I think we should increase our presence within provinces and municipalities, so that people may have easy access to information. It is rather surprising that Canadians are to a great extent ignorant of their own country. This is due in part to the government, the school systems of our various provinces which have no serious programs concerning the many dimensions of our country. This is something which should be checked with the provinces and municipalities. Going over my notes earlier I noticed that there have been meetings of the federal and provincial ministers responsible for tourism since 1934, I think that we should go a step further and come closer to ordinary Canadians. An effort should be made to change our attitude which compels us to stay home, instead of traveling to get to meet other Canadians, who, after all, live in the same country, are faced with the same difficulties but in an environment perhaps different from our own.
I would urge the Minister to consider my remarks carefully, to see whether there is a possibility that Tourism Canada might conclude agreements with the provinces and the municipalities. When someone spends all his time shuffling papers, he has no contact with the public. It is not necessarily a question
of spending more money on a program like this one, but rather to make sure that the money is well spent and that the public does benefit from it. Even if huge amounts of money were spent to advertise Tourism Canada, if the promotional literature remains piled up in warehouses or in offices whose address is very often hard to find, not to mention the offices themselves, all that information is useless and the money is not spent or used for the intended purposes.
That is a problem faced by a lot of people who travel throughout the country. Where are those offices? Perhaps there should be agreements with the various hotel chains so as to be in more direct contact with the public and travellers. Crown corporations such as VIA Rail or CN and CP ought to publish brochures on transport facilities available to get to know our country better. There is very little tourism literature available on the Ottawa-Quebec City or Ottawa-Toronto trains. It is possible to get some information from VIA Rail, but precious little is provided about Northern Canada and about prices in the middle North Shore, the lower North Shore and the Gaspe area. Perhaps we should revise our policies so that the public will have ready access to information, and possibly that is our greatest problem right now. There is no need to spend more money, but maybe we should check with Tourism Canada to see whether all the money is well spent through Government measures or by Tourism Canada officials.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make at this point, Mr. Speaker, because the Minister gave us very clear figures when he spoke earlier. Instead of repeating those figures, I think that the important point is to tell the House and the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) that we must change the attitude of the people by getting them to know their country. There are all kinds of support measures which could be brought forward. When I speak of support, I have in mind not just large amounts of money, but also the specific avenues by which Tourism Canada is trying to make people travel within our own borders. In that respect Hon. Members might have cause to hang their heads, because we may be more inclined to travel abroad instead of travelling in this country. We merely have to recall where our own party leaders spend their holidays. Everyone is going south! I appreciate their position, but if we really want Canadian men and women to travel in this country, we should show them the way. Let us compare current temperatures in Vancouver and Montreal. I think that in Vancouver they are now more or less enjoying summer. It may not be Florida, but this is in our country and I feel that Members of Parliament should be an example in that respect. We should be travelling in Canada to a larger extent, but instead we learn from press reports that some of our ministers, or some prominent Canadians involved in the arts, in politics or in industry are vacationing abroad. A change of attitude would be more warranted than appeals for more and more public
April 14, 1983

funding. At this stage, the need would be less for money and more for talent, in order to change the current approach and increase significantly the impact of funding.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, since I understand I have roughly one minute left, I would like that at the next standing committee meeting where tourism will be dealt with, both opposition and Government Members come up with suggestions concerning this matter of changing our attitudes. We might then have an opportunity to evaluate, and assess them, and see what we might be doing for the future, without criticizing whatever has been done and just asking for money. If from both sides we were to put forward realistic programs, we might then reach the same goals and even double the impact, since this would involve talent rather than mere money.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, tomorrow a young woman will be shot to death in Guatemala. She is currently in jail with her five month old twins. Her husband was killed some eight months ago. It is a crime that this should happen any place in the world.
I have written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and asked that he attempt, on behalf of the Canadian House of Commons, to intervene. I am asking Member of Parliament who are here to intervene also, to call the Embassy of Guatemala here in Ottawa, ask them to express to the President of Guatemala our concern over this matter, and ask that he not have this execution or the four others intended to be
proceeded with tomorrow. Let us ask that every effort be extended to try to find a solution to this problem that will ultimately halt the death of people who, because of their political involvement, face the kind of persecution this woman has faced and the threat of death that she now faces.

Madam Speaker, today I want to express my indignation at the squandering of tax dollars. In his report, the Auditor General has confirmed a fact of which we were already aware-the Government has lost all control over the Crown corporations. Perhaps it does not even know how many there are now. Is that not the best evidence of mismanagement in this country? Here are some examples of the shoddy administration and of the waste of public funds. In 1976, the Government invested $3.6 billion in Petro-Canada, claiming that it was ours, but it never said at what price. Petro-Canada even found a way to spend $6.5 million to keep empty offices in Calgary. According to the Financial Times. the profits of Petro-Canada are sheer fiction! I could also

April 14, 1983
mention Air Canada which has recorded a $32 million deficit this year, and the $10 million it has overspent on its head office. I could also talk about Canadair, the latest scandal and a waste of over $2 billion. And what about Mirabel, the white elephant, the real estate firm which pokes fun at Quebecers who were needlessly expropriated?
I will conclude my remarks, Madam Speaker, by saying that the present Government has run out of wind, as evidenced by the pools, and it does not know which way to turn to make Canadians believe its management is sound. subtopic: GUATEMALA-PROTEST AGAINST DEATH SENTENCE FOR MOTHER OF TWINS

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: GUATEMALA-PROTEST AGAINST DEATH SENTENCE FOR MOTHER OF TWINS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I share the concern expressed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), and would like to give a little more detail of the crisis that will occur tomorrow. This problem was brought to my attention by Amnesty International. The person involved is Dr. Graviola Ruth Brooks Martinez, a general medical practitioner. She is scheduled for execution tomorrow morning in Guatemala. Dr. Martinez is the mother of five-month old twins who are presently in prison with her. Her husband was killed before the twins were born.
The alleged offence is unknown, due to the secrecy of the special military trial that was conducted. Dr. Martinez is the first woman sentenced to death by the Guatemalan military tribunals since the creation of these military tribunals when a state of siege was imposed on Guatemala in July, 1982.
I would like to request the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), on behalf of all Canadians, to protest urgently and in the strongest possible terms against this inhuman, unjust and evil sentence which was based on a trial conducted without legal safeguards. I ask this in the hope that there might be a stay of execution for Dr. Martinez, thereby sparing her life and also providing some security for the welfare of her infant twins.
The Guatemalan Embassy denies that these executions are planned. I fervently hope that this is true, but previous experiences have shown that the Guatemalan embassies have not always been accurately informed by their Government.

Madam Speaker, over four months ago the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) announced policy that would protect the Canadian shipbuilding industry and stimulate activity in the yards. The policy was welcomed by the industry as being meaningful.
Four months have lapsed and the Government has given no indication why introduction has been delayed or when the shipyards and the workers can expect the policy to be implemented. This is four months lost at a time when such policies are urgently needed, at a time when more and more shipyard workers are losing their jobs and fearing for their future.
At the Saint John shipyard employment has decreased from 2,089 in 1978 to only 820 last year. The projected figures for 1983 see a decrease to between 200 and 300 workers this year if no further work is received. This is a scenario that can be prevented.
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) implied Canadian shipbuilders were crybabies who wanted the Government to lead them by the hand. I say this is not so. These men want to work, and want security for themselves and for their families. The Government has tantalized the industry with a program that would get shipbuilding workers back on the job and reverse the shipbuilding decline in Saint John and all across Canada, but has failed to follow through.
On behalf of Canadian shipbuilders I strongly urge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to quit fiddling around and use next Tuesday's budget to introduce the shipbuilding policy and get our workers back to work.

subtopic: NECESSITY FOR INFRASTRUCTURE IN MIDDLE AND LOWER NORTH SHORE, P.Q.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House on a section of my constituency which is on the North Shore, that is the middle and the lower North Shore, with respect to air transport. I would like the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) who has done so many things to this date for the middle and lower North Shore to become aware of the need to set up infrastructures as far as navigational aids are concerned in order to organize landings and take-offs at four main airports of the middle and lower North Shore, that is in the Havre-St-Pierre, Natashquan, la Cheverie and Blanc-Sablon areas. I would also like to point out to the House that some assistance should be provided to the provincial government with respect to the Saint-Augustin airport because in an Indian Reserve last week,
April 14, 1983

a newborn baby died as a result of severe weather conditions due to the lack of a landing strip or ground instruments. Consequently, it is vital that Transport Canada should become acquainted with the needs of that area. We know that for the past three years, tremendous amounts of money have been spent there but even if runways were asphalted, without a system of ground instruments to allow landings and take-offs, the situation is hopeless. This area is situated opposite Newfoundland and considering weather conditions, a system of ground intruments should be a priority. I think that the matter could be dealt with during the negotiations between Quebecair, Nordair and Air Canada. It is very important to consider the entire vital issue, since there are no roads in that part of Canada.

Madam Speaker, at a time when farmers are being stressed to the limit by increasing costs of production and all indications are that world prices will not increase this year, the Canadian Wheat Board Minister is allowing the initial prices for grains to plummet, instead of holding prices at last year's levels. Initial prices for 1983-84 are down 12 cents a bushel for the base grade of wheat, 33 cents for feed barley, and 23 cents for feed oats. Depressed prices such as these are in no way justified at this time.
With farm bankruptcies doubling out West since last year, and such things as fuel, fertilizer and spray prices constantly increasing, how can any farmer look to the 1983-84 crop year with any optimism? To add insult to injury, the Wheat Board Minister, without batting an eye, told farmers the Government wants a 5 per cent reduction in wheat acreage and a 15 per cent reduction in barley acreage. These farmers cannot afford to cut back their production if they are to meet their debt payments.
When competing countries ask their farmers to cut back production they assist the producers with their treasuries. In Canada, as usual, the Liberals place this extra burden on the backs of those least able to afford it, in this case the farmers.
I could not believe my ears yesterday when the Minister of Transport answered a question with, "At the price level at which they are, the general view is that the incentive to produce is still quite high." I want to assure the House that this is a Liberal view and not a general view.

maintopic: S O. 21 RAILWAYS CROWSNEST PASS RATE-GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING IN SUPPORT OF CHANGES
S O. 21 RAILWAYS CROWSNEST PASS RATE-GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING IN SUPPORT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to a major public advertising campaign which the Liberal Party is undertaking this weekend to promote changes to Crowsnest Pass freight rates.
I am informed that the Liberal Party has placed a four-page colour advertising supplement in newspapers in Ontario and western Canada. The commercial rate for this ad in one of the newspapers alone is $9,200. Obviously the total cost for ad production and newspaper space will be well in excess of the $350,000 estimated by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House on February 22.
Our Party regards this as a flagrant waste of public money to promote the policies of the Liberal Party. We find it doubly reprehensible that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is attempting to buy legitimacy for a policy that has been so universally repudiated in western Canada.
These advertisements are also misleading. For example, they promise 375,000 person years of work on the railways, while on May 1 Canadian National will be laying off 837 workers in shops in Winnipeg, Montreal, and Moncton.
This is typical Liberal Party advertising. Its slogan is, "Promise anything. The truth comes later and can never fully catch up."
Madam Speaker, that may be true, until the next general election.

Madam Speaker, the objective of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program may be quite desirable, and undoubtedly many Canadians have benefited from it, but there is one aspect of its administration that requires correction.
Instances have been brought to my attention when applicants were forced by the Department of Manpower and Immigration to take more money from the Government than their actual moving expenses even when they, being honourable citizens, did not want it. All they wanted was reimbursement of their out of pocket expenses. They did not want to profit at the taxpayers' expense.
Letters to the Minister have brought about an almost incomprehensible reply boiling down to "rules are rules and must be enforced regardless of how silly they might be".
It is high time that the regulations governing the Canada Manpower Mobility Program be amended so as to restrict payments to a maximum of the actual out of pocket relocation expenses.

April 14, 1983
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who is no doubt aware of a certain program aired on the CBC last night, touching on Canadair. It included the statement that in October, 1982, he and Members of his Cabinet were informed that the full range of federal involvement in Canadair would be from $1.8 billion to $2.3 billion. In that report it was also made clear that, indeed, Canadair was on the ropes.
Would the Prime Minister inform the House if, in truth, that was the report that was received by him and his Cabinet and, if so, would he care to elaborate on it today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to answer the question, but I have to point out that it is not within the rules to ask the Government if such and such a report is correct or not. A news report is something which should stand by itself. I did not see the program as I was busy with other things and could not watch television.
It is true that the problem of Canadair has been one with which the Government has been concerned. It is also true that when we took the measure to transfer the management of Canadair to the CDIC it was done because we wanted to see business judgment applied to a business difficulty. Therefore, we know that there are difficulties with it.
There is a likelihood that we will have to come to Parliament and ask for a supplementary estimate to assist Canadair in order to turn it into a profitable business venture. I foresee that Parliament will be able to discuss the question at that time.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I wonder if the Prime Minister could indicate if the total federal Government involvement - in short, the people of Canada - in Canadair may reach $1.8 billion, or possibly $2.3 billion?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I cannot confirm those figures. I can give the assurance that if we do come to Parliament for a supplementary estimate we will want to make sure that the financial statements of the company are made available to Parliament so that it can check them.

Madam Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister
of Justice who will undoubtedly be aware that the same program contained the following comment:
Unusual deals have been referred to the Department of Justice for investigation and it in turn has asked the Toronto law firm of Goodman and Goodman to look into some of the contracts.
Would the Minister confirm or otherwise if contracts entered into by Canadair are being examined? Specifically, could he elaborate on the contract between KRS and Canadair, which seems to be strange indeed, bearing in mind that it involves the lease of a Challenger aircraft back to the factory and the possible financing of it by the Government of Canada for certain executives of Pepsi? Is this indeed the Pepsi challenge?
He is over there.
Here comes Brand X.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the context in which the allegation is made by the Hon. Member is substantially untrue. The truth is that legal advice was given through the Department of Justice and through the engagement of outside counsel on, I believe, a single contract. This was not an investigation of any illegality or anything of that kind; it was normal advice given with respect to the interpretation of a contract. That is the only involvement of the Department of Justice in this whole matter.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who was responsible for Canadair at the time, told CBC that no member of his government could have agreed to the lay-off of 7,000 employees of Canadair because of the referendum. What I want to know is whether this means, and Canadians would be happy to be informed in this regard, that the Prime Minister or his government had decided to throw away the taxpayers' money to save the face of the Liberal government at the time of the referendum?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, it is not at all what this means. It simply means that, like any other country which is interested in maintaining a presence in the aeronautical industry, Canada must invest public funds in the industry. This was at the bottom of this whole affair when the private sector did not seem to be able or to want to maintain a Canadian presence in this industry. The Canadian Government did what the government of any other industrialized country would do, I believe, and decided to provide public funds to guarantee a Canadian presence in this
April 14, 1983

high technology industry which is of major importance for the industrial development of Canada.

The Prime Minister should also know that the Minister responsible at the time stated yesterday that he had received a report from the company and that the Cabinet was already aware of its financial problems. In view of the circumstances and since the Minister accepted the proposal of Mr. Lear on a simple phone call, does the Prime Minister not recognize the unprecedented incompetence of his Minister in making such a commitment on behalf of his government, and will the Prime Minister have at least the decency to say so publicly today and invite the Minister to resign because of his incredible incompetence which will cost the Canadian taxpayers billions of dollars? To what extent is the Prime Minister willing to comment publicly on the incredible attitude of the Minister?

I am willing to comment on this attitude, Madam Speaker, and I shall do so in the context that I mentioned earlier when I gave my first reply, namely that we knew that the industry was in difficulty. If such had not been the case, the private sector would not have asked us whether we were willing to get involved in this company. The private sector would have continued to operate and to make profits for its shareholders. Therefore we knew that the company was having problems, and as I just told the Hon. Member, the question for the Government was whether we should let this important sector of the Canadian aeronautical industry in Quebec go under or whether we should try to maintain the presence of the Government, in other words of the Canadian people, in the industry. This was the decision we had to make. The Minister was certainly aware that there was a risk since the private sector wanted to get rid of its assets. The Cabinet's decision at that time was to maintain a Canadian presence in the industry. I would be surprised if the Hon. Member really wanted me to dismiss a Minister because the Canadian Government wanted to use a joint venture, and such ventures have been a Canadian tradition since the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, to keep a high technology industry in Canada with the assistance of public funds. If Sir John A. Macdonald could do so for the railroad, I do not see why the Progressive Conservative Member would not want us to do the same for the aeronautical industry.
Madam Speaker, John A. Macdonald did it for the CPR, as the Prime Minister knows.

Cabinet, and I certainly will not undertake to make those documents public. The Cabinet system works on a system of confidentiality. Advice we receive from officials operates on that basis. speechtext:
I see the Member for Joliette wants to put in his two cents' worth, Madam Speaker! Perhaps you could recognize him later on, since he forgot to phrase his questions properly just now. Perhaps the Hon. Member would have the courtesy to let me answer the Member on the other side, who did not interrupt him when he was asking his questions.

I have recognized that the company was in difficulty. I have recognized that we had to make a very important decision there, whether to cut loose from support of the aeronautic industry in Canada, particularly in the case of Canadair, or whether we should try to find some way to ensure that better commercial decisions were made by that company. What we have done, as is known by the House, is transfer the assets to a Crown corporation operating in the commercial sector, and we believe that there will be better decisions in matters of commercial decisions taken by the CDIC than could be taken in the previous circumstances.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM ON COMPANY'S DEBT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister has a different notion about the responsibility of Government to the people of Canada than we have on this side of the House. We believe the people of Canada are spending millions, indeed billions of dollars, and they ought to know how that money is being spent. That is the issue.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM ON COMPANY'S DEBT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, since it has been quite seriously alleged that this company has given literally millions of dollars to a private American corporation, that this company's senior management has misled a committee of this House, that this company in fact, if the allegation is true, is overcharging the Government of Canada for these planes while undercharging private corporations-given all of these allegations would the Prime Minister do what he ought to do, use the authority of the Inquiries Act and set up a thorough, competent, and fair-minded public investigation into this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Once again, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party is not interested in the subject; he is interested in the
process. He says the people ought to know how their dollars are being spent. If he had listened to my previous answers he would have seen that I said exactly the same thing and that I think the House of Commons will have an opportunity to see how the dollars are being spent. But why this leads him to ask to look at the Cabinet documents, Madam Speaker, just shows that he is trying to bring a red herring into the subject.
You are bringing in the red herring.
He is trying to see a scandal where there may or may not be one.
We want to know.

Exactly. That is why I said the House will be in a position to look at the figures. We intend at that point to bring the financial statements down and have the Opposition ask every legitimate question. After that, if they think, and if it is obvious, that there should be room for an inquiry, we will look at that question.
Once again, there is an admission by the Government that we took over a failing company and it was deeply in trouble. The only question at this stage that I can answer is that the Government, rather than cut it loose and see another industry die in Canada, a high technology industry, decided to try to find some way of saving it. I should have thought that the NDP, of all parties, would not have objected to the Government of Canada trying to save a high technology industry, and do it in a rational way.
Hear, hear!

Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs.

April 14, 1983
