subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister said earlier that he did not have time to watch television last night. It is a sad day when Members of the Opposition have to watch television to find out what on earth is going on within the Government backrooms of this country.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: How sad for you.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is well known that the Government appointed a special task force in 1981 to look into the financial fiasco surrounding Canadair and the Challenger aircraft. The Prime Minister has indicated that the Cabinet received a document in October, presumably outlining a number of the problems. So is it fair to assume, on behalf of Members opposite, that the Cabinet, and perhaps the Government itself, were well aware of the difficulties and the fiasco surrounding both the financial and marketing aspects of Canadair?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member did not waste his time watching television he would have heard me say that very thing in the House just a moment ago. He is so obsessed with what he saw on the airwaves that he did not hear me say, yes, that was one of the great worries of the Government and that is why we took the steps I indicated to have better business judgment put into this matter. That is why we transferred the assets of Canadair to the CDIC.
As I put it in previous statements, the matter is really- should the Canadian people, the Canadian Government and, particularly, the NDP lose their nerve when there are difficulties in areas of high technology? We know that these-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: You've got to be joking.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: -difficulties exist in the United States, they exist in Germany, they exist in France and they exist in Britain in the aeronautic industry. It is not a very profitable industry at this time, and the real question-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: Buy a restaurant next time.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT TASK FORCE-KNOWLEDGE OF CANADA1R AFFAIRS
speechtext: -we had to address was: do we lose our nerve and bail out, or do we stay in and try to make a better turn of events? We took the second option, and that is why we turned the assets over to the CDIC.

Madam Speaker, a few months back, Canadair came to Parliament Hill with a
number of slick presentations about the Challenger aircraft. Canadair also appeared before each of the caucuses, clearly explaining how well it was doing. Canadair appeared before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, again to explain its case, while it requested an additional $200 million in borrowing.
At that time it was very clear that Canadair knew of the financial difficulties and this rather shameful attempt at marketing in which it was involved. Government Members opposite knew, yet nothing was said during all of those presentations and all of those hearings and not a single iota of information that was presented last night on television came out.
Can the Prime Minister tell us is this not really saying that the Government Members opposite, the Cabinet opposite, and Canadair purposely misled the House of Commons and, therefore, the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member described it as being a shameful attempt at marketing. Obviously, the Canadair executives were in the business of marketing a product.
Why didn't they explain it to us then?
I do not think it would have been a good marketing approach to come and say that it was a terrible aircraft, that it could not fly, and that nobody should buy it.
Television's the way to introduce it; is that it?

Madam Speaker, television has done, I understand, a responsible job in reporting the facts as it sees them, but does not have to make the decision which I said the Government had to make, and that I wonder how the NDP would have made.
We want it from you, rather than television.
Well, give us the information. We'll tell you.

If the Leader of the NDP would once again listen, I said that we would give the information, that he would have the figures, that the financial figures would be brought before Parliament. I do not happen to have them today. I do not think they are ready. My understanding is that the year end is June 30, not December 31.
They changed it.

I do not have them today, and I do not have them just because, by happenstance, television happened to have a program last night. Parliament will have to follow its own processes and not only be guided by the timing of television.

Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and relates to a program announced in the spring of 1981 which was called the Caribbean Basin Initiative. It was to include all countries of the region and to exclude military activities of any sort. Now, after two years, I would like to know what this Basin Initiative has meant to the developing countries of the region. Also, in view of the huge military involvement of the USA in the region, I would like to know if we are still willing to be part of that program.
Tell us about the Soviets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the full Caribbean Basin Initiative has not yet been legislated in the United States. The aid component has been approved by Congress, but the trade and investment portions, to my knowledge, have not yet been approved by Congress, so that the five participating countries have not yet been in a position to implement the over-all initiative which, in our view, had the advantage of increasing, by a very substantial amount, American aid to the Caribbean countries and which, if implemented, would open access, without tariffs, by the American markets to these Caribbean countries.
In our view the Caribbean initiative stands on its own feet as a valuable, constructive effort to assist the economy and social structure of these countries. It is not, in our view, associated with any military or security thrust, either.
That's baloney.

Member for Yukon could find out that there is something called "usual channels" to discuss the matter between the various House Leaders.

subsubtopic: CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: The Prime Minister, if I am to take him sincerely, believes that Parliament should deal with the matter. He seems unwilling to submit that which he has referred to in his previous answers as a matter which may be a scandal to a special committee of this House which would have no other responsibility than to look into the matter. Will he, then, adopt the impartial and responsible course of agreeing to a special order of the House to refer the matter to the Auditor General for a focused and special study in order that he, as an impartial servant of the House, may report his findings to Parliament?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I take the opposite view to that of the Hon. Member. There may have been some business judgments which could have been taken or should have been taken otherwise. That will be a matter for the House to examine. I suggest that, after that, the concern of the Hon. Member and his suspicions should be brought to the fore, and then we will decide whether there should be a special inquiry of one kind, or not.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Cabinet has authorized our ambassador in Washington, Allan Gotlieb, to expend, as a beginning, the sum of $650,000 to engage lobbyists in Washington. Is it true that our relationships with the United States are deteriorating to the

April 14, 1983
Oral Questions
extent that we must now hire American public relations firms to represent our country in Washington?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES-HIRING OF LOBBYISTS IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think that the conclusion of the Hon. Member is justified. I think that if he has been following, for example, the efforts of both the Governments of Manitoba and Canada in support of the Canadian objectives on the Garrison Diversion, he would have known that both Governments have retained the services of a professional lawyer in Washington to assist in that particular project.
In particular instances of that kind where Canadian interests are involved, it has proved useful to engage local professionals who know the scene and know how to carry the requirement objectives of the Government of Canada forward. I think it was rather a good idea, myself.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES-HIRING OF LOBBYISTS IN WASHINGTON
speechtext: I take it from the answer given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that there is no point in having any diplomatic representation there. All one does is hire American public relations firms to represent Canada-to line up with the National Rifle Association or Friends of the Earth.

Madam Speaker, does the Secretary of State for External Affairs consider this allocation of funds, which is just a beginning, as a reflection on the competence of the foreign service officers who are representing Canada in the United States, and can he say whether or not he thinks there is any point now in building Erickson's palace to house all these public servants to represent Canada? Can they not do the job and deal with Congressmen, or is it necessary now to hire public relations firms?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member continues to demonstrate his ignorance of the complexity and the diversity of the relations that exist between Canada and the United States. I have the greatest confidence in the professional capacity of the embassy staff, all of whom are doing a first rate job. It was on the evaluation provided by the embassy in the first instance that this particular initiative has been approved by the Government of Canada, which was recommended to the Government by myself.
Now I understand.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Hon. Member ought to understand that the sum of money which he has indicated is just another indication of his ignorance of what is happening in Washington.

subsubtopic: CANADAIR-REQUEST THAT INDEPENDENT INQUIRY BE ESTABLISHED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. I would like to return to the Canadair matter. Surely the issue here is the need to divulge all the information on this Canadair matter, whether it is a scandal, bad business judgment, or whatever.
Surely the Government cannot be a judge in its own case. Would the Prime Minister agree that what is being questioned here is not just the mismanagement of the company but the Government's handling of the affair which is being criticized? Therefore it is not sufficient to wait for the estimates to come in front of the House. Without an independent inquiry in the matter, the Government simply gives whatever information it wants and is, indeed, the judge in its own case.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: CANADAIR-REQUEST THAT INDEPENDENT INQUIRY BE ESTABLISHED
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I do not agree with the Hon. Member.

Madam Speaker, I will rephrase the question to the Prime Minister so he can perhaps understand it. We are dealing with CDIC which is responsible for Canadair. We are dealing with Senator Jack Austin who is responsible for Canadair, but we cannot question him in the House of Commons. We are dealing with a Government that seems to believe in excessive secrecy.
If the Prime Minister wants to be fair, as he has indicated, and wants to get all the information out on this important matter, and if he has nothing to hide, why will he not allow a public inquiry so that we can put all these questions? For the good of public enterprise in the future we can get all the information out and show the Canadian public that these enterprises can indeed be run properly.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again the Hon. Member seems to ignore the answers that I gave to the previous questions. We in the Government intend to put these figures out. The Government intends to have the financial statements looked at by the Opposition, but I explained that we do not have the financial statements now. I believe they are due at the end of June.
Today I was discussing with the officers of the company the possibility of getting them out earlier so that Parliament could indeed look into this matter.
Those are the steps I have taken. That is the pledge that I give. If we can get the financial statements out earlier, we will do so. The Opposition will then be in a position to ask its questions on the basis of real facts.
As I said in answer to the first question, we recognize that they will find a very distressing financial situation calling for a basic decision, either the injection of more funds-which is why I talked of supplementary estimates-or a bailing out completely.
April 14, 1983

Once again, I would think that on this subject we would at least have a temporary understanding from the NDP and that they would set partisanship aside for the moment and remember their own philosophy.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have great pleasure in introducing this Bill, an Act to amend the Holidays Act. The purpose of this Bill is to emphasize the fact that the constitutional independence of Canada was achieved on April 17, 1982 by the proclamation of the Canada Act, 1982. This day should therefore be celebrated in the future as Canada Day. The naming of July 1, marking the beginning of the Dominion of Canada, as it was known in 1867, would be restored to its historically more appropriate name of Dominion Day.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gass:

April 14, 1983

That the House condemns the Government for its neglect of the Canadian tourist industry and calls upon the Government to recognize this industry as a major generator of employment, new economic growth, and foreign exchange and that the Government accept its responsibility to increase the visibility of Canadian tourism both at home and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, a year ago, but for two years, Queen Elizabeth II signed the Constitution Act. It was said that that Act was typically Canadian and that it was a compromise among all Parties. One must assume that the Government feels that it is a typical compromise with regard to tourism since no special Minister or special Department heads up tourism. Indeed it has been allocated to the Minister responsible for small business. If it has to be under the auspice of some Minister as a part time job, I am delighted it is with the Minister who represents that delightful part of Newfoundland and Labrador. However, it does not give the significance to that particular industry that it deserves.
Before lunch the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) adequately set out the jobs, the dollars, the lack of Government support and other points necessary to set the tone for those of us who follow him to expand on. Briefly let me indicate that this afternoon I will speak on behalf of my riding of Prince Edward-Hastings, but I would like to expand it slightly to include all of Hastings since the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Vankough-net) will not have an opportunity to speak on this matter, and as he in the past has adequately represented my feelings on gun legislation and other matters, I know I speak for him when it comes to tourism in that part of Ontario.
There is no specific thrust for this second largest Canadian industry. There was very little for the first, especially when we consider that the timber industry has no Minister as well. The things which happen in the area of tourism continue to depress me. For example, recently a marina in the Bay of Quinte asked for a small business investment grant. The man very rightly wanted to use that money to purchase used equipment rather than brand-new equipment, and he was told by another Minister that it could not be done under the regulations. Surely a Minister completely responsible for tourism would have undertaken his cause, seen the sensible approach he was taking and as an advocate looked after the matter.
There is another marina called the Baycrest Marina which is dealing with the Small Craft Harbours Branch of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. While the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) is a very decent chap, he is not much concerned about marinas in the Bay of Quinte. This is not a reflection upon Mr. Moffat and his staff. As a matter of fact they were recently helpful in another harbour in Prince Edward Country, the Wellington Harbour. It is the only harbour on the west coast of Prince Edward County where the direct winds from Lake Ontario beat against it and it is necessary to have a safe harbour for sailing ships. The Small Craft Harbours Branch has approved a grant to study the opening up of this particular harbour. Just so that no one will think I am hitting at one Government only, let me make the point that the Province of Ontario has not been very cooperative in picking up the other half. We may be able to get some funds out of the Province before we are done.
The Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) mentioned this morning that the extra cost of gasoline was a very important factor in deterring tourists from coming into the area. In Prince Edward-Hastings drivers who come up from the United States are still working on tanks of fuel which they purchased there. It does not matter whether we are talking litres or gallons, United States or Canadian dollars; when they fill up their tanks at stations in the Belleville area, they remember very clearly what dollars they spent in the United States and they know very well that they are spending more money in Canada.
Also this morning TIAC was mentioned. For the record that is the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, which has done a tremendous amount of work and has co-operated very well with the Hon. Member for Malpeque. Referring to the study which it put before the Government some time ago, it indicated that Governments seemed to have the philosophy that people should not really enjoy themselves, that therefore it was fair to heap extra taxes on items such as meals, liquor and hotel rooms, and that they failed to realize the provision and sale of these items provided employment for 10 per cent of our work force. That 10 per cent or the one million people about whom we talked this morning indicates the size of the tourism industry.
The spirits industry is very important in Prince Edward-Hastings. We have a large distiller there. It seems to me that there is a lack of concentration on the tourism aspect of this industry. The indexation of federal taxes on the spirits industry at present is such that just last year the returns to the federal Government started to decrease. They have finally broken the camel's back. They have added taxes to the point where the return to the federal Government is now decreasing. I hope in the forthcoming budget next week that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) will take a look at this very unpopular and unfair tax. I do not think there is anyone in the House or throughout the land who does not agree that the taxing of those vices which some of us enjoy is fair game for Government. When we consider that $400 million worth of distillery business brings in $1.6 billion of taxes to both levels of Government, we have some idea of the inequity. I doubt there is any other industry of which it could be said that the taxes total four times its gross income.
Distillers are the only segment of the entire food industry which has to submit its labels to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for approval before they are put on their products. Sometimes this approval is held up for eight to 12 weeks. This may sound like a very small matter but when one is in a business which is as competitive and price conscious as the distillery business, one has some idea that a hold up of eight to 12 weeks on labels is not required by any other part of the industry and is totally unfair.
Once again, if I am to be fair to the different levels of Government, the provincial laws are not much better when it comes to bars and that sort of thing. Bars are closed on
April 14, 1983

election day, as all of us know. That brings about inequities which are very difficult to stomach. The most recent byelection which comes to mind was the one in the Spadina riding in Toronto when bars on one side of the street were open and the ones on the other side of the street were closed. Surely we must get away from this. American tourists coming into Ontario would not be aware of a by-election and they certainly would not be impressed if they had to change restaurants from one side of the street to the other just to have a drink.
The Province of Ontario has just completed a study which is of major importance to the tourism industry in Prince Edward County. West Lake Lodge is in the throes of being brought back. While it means very little to people in this House, nonetheless to people in the area it is of great importance.
One of the criticisms I have of the federal Government is that there are no tax incentives to allow, assist or encourage a private entrepreneur to get involved in the tourist industry. The Minister mentioned this morning the need for individuals to assist in tourism. I say to the Minister that there is a need for some encouragement. I suggest that encouragement come by way of tax incentives to help private entrepreneurs develop the tourist industry. There has been no growth in accommodation in the tourist industry for many years.
Prince Edward County is a part of the Prince Edward-Hastings constituency. It is not unlike the Prince Edward Island of my colleague from Malpeque. It is a blessed, beautiful area with lakes and beaches. I tell my friend from Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) that we have miles and miles of beaches in Prince Edward County, some of them untouched by man for weeks, months and perhaps years at a time. It is a rural area with orchards. If I had the ability to describe the scene from Lake of the Mountain, looking at the Bay of Quinte, I would indeed be eloquent, but I cannot. It is one of the most beautiful parts of all of Canada. We are prepared to share that area. It would indeed be profitable to share that area with tourists. It would not only be profitable for the local people but profitable for the federal Government. Tourism is like the goose that lays the golden egg: it is in danger of being killed.
In 1984 we will celebrate the 200th anniversary of the landing of the Loyalists in that part of Canada. It will be a year of celebration, a very exciting and historic time. I know that the Province is participating. I know of some of the student programs which I approved in the past few weeks and sent on to the proper Minister. These projects will lead up to that.
The Minister about whom I said such nice words a few moments ago has now entered the House. He might reciprocate and prove me slightly wrong by taking part in this tremendous and exciting celebration of the landing of the Loyalists. It would be a time for the Government tourism office to show its sincerity and get deeply involved.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Tourism Canada.

Make it Tourism Canada. We will put that on all the flags, providing that it gets involved in this anniversary.

Mr. Speaker it is indeed a pleasure for me to speak today on a very important industry in Canada, tourism and the tourist industry. Long gone are the days when tourists flocked in avalanche numbers to Canada from the United States and many other countries of the world. Some call them the good old days. Long gone are the days when tourists were taken as a matter of course, were taken for granted, that we were doing them a favour to let them into our country and leave their holiday money with us.
Long done are the days when our operators and tourist personnel really did not extend themselves, did not really practise good hospitality, did not really practise friendliness, in many cases provided only mediocre accommodation and served unappetizing food. They were not too concerned whether the tourist would come back another time, not interested in repeat business, as there were always plenty of other tourists to take their place.
Today, perhaps because of our economic crisis, perhaps because there are other more hospitable and more tourist-oriented countries which know the great potential of tourism and the positive effect a thriving tourist industry has on their total economy, but whatever the reason, we have not been holding up our end in attracting more tourists to our country.
Some countries actively cultivate and greatly depend on the foreign exchange earned through tourism to keep their economy viable. Over the years I have had the good fortune to visit many countries around the world. I am sure many of my colleagues have had the same opportunity. I was always impressed by the courteous, hospitable and friendly way in which I was received and attended to, whether I was shopping, in a restaurant, hotel or any other place. I was always left with the good feeling and the desire that some day I would like to revisit those countries and relive and enjoy their outstanding hospitality and friendliness.
Many of those countries, to encourage an even greater flow of tourism to their country, give special concessions to tourists in the form of vouchers to purchase gasoline at a cheaper rate, special rates on accommodations, travelling, special rates on sightseeing, etc., all kinds of gambits to cultivate and encourage this very important industry. This is what Canada has to compete with and emulate if we are to improve our tourist industry and encourage more people to visit our country.
Although international tourism has grown substantially in the past decade, Canada did not share to any great extent in this growth. For example, the number of visitors entering Canada from the United States fell some 7.5 million in 1982, mainly because of a decrease in short-term automobile traffic.
Long-term U.S. visitors numbered 10.9 million in 1982, down almost 4 per cent from the year before. In contrast to this, the number of Canadians leaving the country totalled 34.8 million in 1982. In fact, the relative growth in travel outside Canada has resulted in a tourist deficit for us ranging

April 14, 1983
Supply
between $1 and $2 billion a year since the mid-1970s. The latest forecasts indicate that Canada's travel deficit could rise over $2 billion annually by as early as 1987 if something is not done to curtail the trend.
Many of the factors affecting Canadian tourism, like the changing economic climate, energy issues and travellers' attitudes and expectations, are some of the things that we and the tourist industry have to come to grips with. Another reality is the fierce competition for tourist dollars worldwide. As more and more countries develop their tourist industries, we have to work harder, much harder, to maintain and hopefully increase our current market share.
I seem to sense that one of the difficulties that has to be overcome is to get it across that tourist operators are not the only ones who benefit by the tourist dollar, but that retail businesses, such as restaurants, shops, hotels and motels, get the highest percentage of the tourist dollar. These outlets have a direct responsibility to become more active than they are now in greater promotion locally and nationally of tourism.
Collingwood in my constituency, which is noted as a ski resort in the winter, because of the lack of snow a couple of years ago suffered a considerable set back to its economy during that season. Even this year the lack of sufficent snow had an adverse effect in the community. Every businessman complained of lack of business. One thing it did bring out most forcibly is how much the town really depended economically on the ski business in the winter. It also served to increase substantially financial support and interest for the promotion of tourism in the area.
In the area around Owen Sound and in Grey and Bruce Counties, tourism is estimated to be worth $250 million and generates some 10,000 jobs. Even with this, some people in the area, according to the Owen Sound Sun Times, are still surprised to hear that tourism is here and wonder why Government should support the industry. I believe what needs to be done is to make people more aware of the importance of tourism and how everybody in a tourist area benefits either directly or indirectly, and that they do everything possible to maintain and expand it.
It is important too that people work together, not at cross purposes with each other. Resources for promotion and advertising should be pooled, have one good organization locally and be fully supported. Duplicating efforts is both timeconsuming and generally less productive. Some people still do not understand or are not aware that tourism in Canada is big business, despite our mediocre supportive ways for the industry. In 1981 tourism generated over $28 billion of income and provided employment for over 1,130,000 Canadians. There are approximately 100,000 tourist businesses today in Canada. I believe this is a firm base on which to build and to regenerate the industry, because there is room for a great deal of improvement.
These improvements should start to take place as soon as next year. In 1984 we will be observing the 450th anniversary of the arrival of Jacques Cartier in Canada, and 1984 will also
be the bicentenary of the United Empire Loyalist settlement in Ontario. All these events and others are a spin-off for tourism and we should take account of them. As the Minister said, 1984 also marks the 50th anniversary of the co-operation of federal and provincial governments and the Canadian tourism industry in the growth and development of tourism. The first federal Government agency entirely devoted to tourism was established in 1934.
We hope that all these events and others will give tourism all across our country a much needed shot in the arm and the impetus to raise the whole tourist industry to even greater heights. However, Mr. Speaker, rhetoric alone without concrete physical support for the tourist industry will not suffice to bolster the industry.
The owners of the existing 190,000 hotel and resort rooms, the 29,000 cabins across the country, the 78,000 motel rooms, are all facing the same critical problem-the inability to generate new capital for repairs and expansion. In each Province today there are millions of dollars worth of projects that are unable to proceed because of this financial crisis. The banking community has shown little interest in this problem and has largely refused any assistance, considering the tourist industry on the whole as very risky. It is up to the federal and provincial Governments to take a more active role in this area and to come forth with the financial assistance that is so badly needed.
In Ontario alone in 1981 $600 million worth of tourist resort building and renovations were halted due to financial difficulties. This has resulted in the loss of 17,000 construction jobs and 5,270 permanent operational jobs.
Despite the size of the tourist industry in Canada, the federal Government and the Provinces have not given attention to this multibillion dollar industry equal to that given to the forestry, mining and fisheries industries. This in itself has a negative impact on investors' confidence in the marketplace. The result is that there is a desperate lack of both capital and mortgage funds for tourist resort projects in all parts of the country. High interest rates and the declining economy have not helped either.
I believe the federal Government has a duty to support the tourism industry in a more aggressive manner. New life has to be breathed into the resort construction industry, possibly in the form of tax incentive measures and other measures that would contribute to the betterment of the industry so that it can attract a larger share of the Canadian and international tourist spending.
With the better availability of equity funds the Canadian tourism industry will be better able to develop to its full potential. It has been estimated that the right mix of tax incentives could encourage about $1.5 billion of annual construction. This construction activity plus the future employment in the tourist facilities will, in turn, generate substantial tax revenues to the federal Government. It has been estimated that the cost of providing the tax incentives will be substantially less than the future revenue generated.
April 14, 1983

Without positive solutions many more Canadian resort operators, resort hotels and resort facilities will be bankrupt in 1984. To facilitate more federal involvement I would like to see a separate department of tourism set up with its own minister in charge. Tourism is and can reach an even greater potential when full focus is applied to the tourism industry, as would happen if it had its own entity in the Cabinet. I believe the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) has voiced approval of such an undertaking. It is to be hoped that this will be approved by Cabinet as it would indeed result in a better deal for the operators, more permanent work for their employees and a better and a more attractive deal for tourists.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize the importance of having good, pleasant, friendly personnel serving the needs of tourists. Nothing turns anyone off more than sloppy service, slovenly and unkempt personal presentation, poor accommodation and often poor food. All efforts should be made to rectify these problems where they apply. A happy, contented tourist generates by word of mouth more business in the tourist industry than all the brochures and pictures combined. An unsatisfied and disgruntled tourist can, again by word of mouth, devastate a tourist business, possibly to the point of no return. Brochures will help tourists get to an area but the bottom line and the most important area is service.
As one who grew up in the food business I know that the slogan "The customer is always right" is not an idle one. Everything should be done to ensure that the customers are really being looked after and do indeed receive value for the money spent. A contented customer is a satisfied customer. Repeat business is the lifeblood of any business, including the tourist industry. It is a source of revenue that an operator can count on which influences his cash flow, his buying and his planning. It is also a sign that the operator must be doing something right. On the other hand, if such ingredients are lacking or only partially present, that will indeed spell bankruptcy and doom to those affected. Perhaps that is the way it should be. Perhaps those operators who have no business being in the tourist business in the first place should take their leave of the business so they may be replaced by more experienced people, those with more know-how about tourism, more knowhow about accommodations, more know-how about the preparation of food and meals and how to treat people as important guests in their homes.
I am sure that if all this is accomplished, Mr. Speaker, tourism in Canada will take an upswing toward greater prosperity for the whole tourist industry and tourism.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to make some comments about Canada's growing tourist industry. The motion of the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) reads as follows:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of the Canadian tourist industry and calls upon the Government to recognize this industry as a major generator of employment, new economic growth, and foreign exchange
Supply
and that the Government accept its responsibility to increase the visibility of Canadian tourism both at home and abroad.
The motion is very appropriate when we consider that because of the old-fashioned approach to economic development taken by the Government in the last few years, by and large tourism has been overlooked. An indication of this is the fact that there is no federal department of tourism as such; it is just something that is tacked on to the responsibility of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey). That demonstrates how the Government feels about tourism as a major growth area in the country.
I do not want to cast aspersions just at the federal Government. We see the same thing with most provincial Governments where tourism is an area of minor interest or is handled by a minor department, if indeed there is a department at all.
I know that the Minister feels very strongly about tourism and recognizes it as a potential growth area in the economy. Tourism has a lot of good things going for it, Mr. Speaker. It is a labour-intensive industry. It tends to be family oriented, community oriented and regionally oriented. It is a reflection of the true Canadian spirit. Canada calls to the world to come and visit. Yet those voices are spread throughout the country as a result of a lack of focus, lack of direction and, indeed, because there is no over-all industrial strategy for the country. It does not fall within any framework of an industrial strategy or a national recovery program. There is simply an industry, in a sense, crying out in the wilderness. When people from beyond our borders think of Canada, what images come to their minds? What do people perceive as being Canada? I believe what they perceive is a great country, a country of open spaces, a country which is relatively pollution free, a country of streams and forests and mountains with a kind of pristine environment. Most people in the world today are living in large metropolitan areas, and as any demographer will tell you, in the years ahead more and more of our global citizens will be located in densely populated urban areas which tend to be polluted with industry. Canada, as a clean, pristine, friendly environment becomes more and more an international attraction when it comes to tourists.
First and foremost of Canada's major resources are the people of Canada with their ingenuity, talents, abilities, their expertise and their zest for life. One could even say it is our most critical resource. Our resources which are often overlooked are our location as a country mid-point between Europe and Asia and our relatively clean, pleasant and attractive environment. If we were going to identify a sector which is going to attract foreign currency to the country in the years ahead, I believe tourism is that sector. Twenty years from now tourism will not be a sort of afterthought of Government activities. Tourism will in fact be one of our major thrusts in terms of economic development and job creation in Canada.
It is disturbing to look at our newspapers these days, particularly the weekend supplements, to see that the thrust now is to get Canadians out of Canada and down to the sunny

April 14, 1983
Supply
climes. There are all sorts of deals by all kinds of transportation systems to encourage Canadians to leave Canada. I believe, Mr. Speaker, we should look very carefully at the reasons why people come to Canada. I believe that people come to Canada now, and have in the past, and will likely come in the future because there are some unique experiences which they can have here. Why do they go to Florida, the Caribbean or Mexico at this time of year? Because it is a unique experience. You can get rid of your winter clothes, lie in the sunshine and enjoy the heat. You can enjoy different music, different sounds, different foods. You can have an altogether different experience than you can in a Canadian city, village or rural area.
Why do people come to Canada? I do not believe we have addressed that question adequately, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest to the Minister responsible for tourism that he and his colleagues look very carefully at developing tourist packages so that when tourists leave Canada they leave having had a Canadian experience.
In western Canada we have two languages with respect to our tourist season. They are not French and English; they are English and Japanese. The thousands and thousands of Japanese tourists who are now visiting Canada tend to visit western Canada because they are represented in that cultural landscape through the Japanese language and Japanese catering facilities. When they come to that part of Canada they want to have a unique experience. They want to see a cattle drive, a rodeo or a stampede. They want to see the wide open spaces they do not see in Japan, and they do experience Canada as a place quite different from the heavily populated areas of Japan.
But there is so much more that can be done in terms of taking advantage of the wonderful tourist opportunities which exist in this country. For example, in most parts of Canada there is an opportunity to hunt and fish at certain times of the year. Yet I suspect that across this country today those families or individuals who are developing fishing camps, resorts and hunting lodges are being pushed into bankruptcy.
These are very difficult times for these people. They are hanging on right now, but if there is not some significant turnaround in the economy in the weeks and months ahead, we are going to begin to lose that very critical tourist infrastructure. If these people do not receive some level of assistance and support from Government, Mr. Speaker, we will begin to see the hunting and fishing lodges, and the resorts disappear from the Canadian landscape. And if they do remain in place, they will no longer be the family-oriented enterprise; it will be the international chain which will take over. Who is it that advertises tourist opportunities? Who is it that caters to international tourists? It is too often the national and international chains which operate in Canada. While one may say, thank goodness they are at least doing it, the point is that the small operator is being left out of the action. And I am not certain those small operations can continue to limp along with the inadequate support given by provincial and federal Governments.
It is important, Mr. Speaker, that we look at this industry much more seriously. I believe that a great deal of attention is being paid today to Government grants of one kind or another which provide assistance to the manufacturing sector. We realize that tourism is the one sector of our economy which has eroded in terms of importance and which has never been developed adequately. Existing tax breaks and grant programs tend to be focused almost exclusively on the processing and manufacturing sector. While that focus is well intentioned and, indeed, I feel should be supported, there is still the one sector which is obviously overlooked, that is, tourism. I do not believe there is a Province in Canada which has a healthy tourist infrastructure. I listened not long ago to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) when he was talking about air fares which encourage Canadians to go southward, and he was quite appreciative of these reduced air fares so Canadians could find holiday relief in the United States or other countries. But I do not see that same initiative and encouragement for Canadians to holiday in their own country. As a matter of fact, I see quite the contrary. In the mountainous region of British Columbia where I come from, what has attracted tourists from around the world and is one of the finest tourist experiences which foreign visitors can have is to travel in a domed car from Jasper to Vancouver through the Rocky Mountains, the Coast Mountains and through the interior plateau. It is a fantastic experience. I would say it is one of the most unique experiences in the world. There was also an opportunity to travel by Via Rail, get out at a stop and hike in the Alpine Meadows. Almost inevidently, you will see all kinds of wildlife alongside the train tracks or on a very simple walk up a well developed trail system. The Government has now decided they should cut off that Via Rail arm, and that particular line of track will no longer be open to the tourist traffic. Now, Mr. Speaker, for the Government to say on one hand, "We support tourism, the tourists, the entrepreneur, the developer", and then take away his or her very lifeblood, tends to make those comments ring somewhat hollow. It tends to make people a bit suspicious and cynical about the validity of the Government's intentions, be it federal, provincial or in many cases local.
There is a great deal of work that can be done to encourage the tourism sector. It ought to be done for the reasons I have stated, but there is one other which is perhaps the most important of all in the long term. Of all industrial economic pursuits, the one which tends to favour the long-term preservation of Canada's environment is tourism. That industry has a vested interest in maintaining one of the cleanest, most attractive, unpolluted and pristine environments found anywhere in the world on this scale. You cannot say that about many other sectors of our economy which have had such a devastating impact on the state of the Canadian environment.
Considering the long-term benefits of tourism to Canada, its contribution to our balance of payments and to developing one of the few growth sectors in our economy, I encourage the Government to take to heart today this motion presented by
April 14, 1983

the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass). It should recognize that adequate emphasis has not been placed on this industry and that to generate more and new employment and new economic growth and to improve our foreign exchange picture, the Government would be miles ahead if it provided a very clear and encouraging signal to many Canadians in the upcoming budget by including in it a major component to stimulate, encourage, nurture and recognize the value of the tourism sector of our economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Burghardt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be involved for a few minutes in this debate and say a few things on the Opposition motion presented today. I think when you look at the over-all tourism program which the Government sponsored, you would have to say that, quite to the contrary of what we heard this afternoon, albeit in a positive way, the Government does in fact support in various generous ways the entire tourism industry in Canada. In fact, I was just looking through some material which shows how the Canadian Government Office of Tourism is using its advertising budget to promote tourism in Canada. This campaign is being carried out in many countries such as the United Kingdom, Australia, France, Japan and Germany. I think we are seeing the benefits of that support because we know for a fact that people from foreign lands visit Canada on a far more regular basis than we have experienced in recent years.
Speaking for my own area in south-west Ontario, particularly the City of London, just last weekend the London Free Press, the major newspaper in the area, sponsored a three-day travel Canada seminar, which it has done now for a few years. I think they should be congratulated. Here again the Government of Canada co-operated by setting up a booth on the premises and distributing much worthwhile information. I think about 10,000 people went through this three-day seminar. Not all the Provinces were represented, but Ontario and, I believe, some of the Maritime Provinces were. I do not believe any of the western Provinces were there, and I think that is a shame because here was an opportunity for at least the residents of southwestern Ontario to find out more about what accommodations and tour attractions are available across this great country of ours. I just mention this, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of Hon. Members and to show that there is much going on across this country, certainly in southwestern Ontario and particularly in London, to promote tourism in Canada, all supported by the Government.
As I think has been alluded to this afternoon, we know that tourism in Canada is big business; $15 billion a year, one million jobs and something like 100,000 businesses. When Hon. Members opposite talk about the importance of this industry from the economic standpoint, they are right on target. There is no question about it and no one is denying that. Members on this side of the House equally support greater involvement by the Government and all interested parties in promoting tourism in Canada. We have a great
Supply
country with a lot to offer and there are tremendous opportunities, not only for people to visit, but I think there are tremendous investment opportunities which perhaps private investors should become more interested in.
I think it has been stated that by the year 2000 tourism will be a $500 billion a year global industry. It is estimated that more than two billion people will travel every year. To maintain an increase in Canada's share of this market, our commitment goes beyond just the promotion of Canada as a world travel destination; it extends as well, as I am sure Hon. Members realize, to public awareness campaigns, staff training and hospitality workshops, really to make every visitor a VIP. But I do not think the Government can do it alone. It is up to individual operators to take advantage of some of these programs and, as I believe one Hon. Member mentioned earlier, to keep their facilities in good working order and make sure their staff maintains a pleasant and presentable front to the visitors who might be making use of their facilities.
I think the Canadian Government has shown it is committed to the development of Canada's tourist industry, and the public and private sectors together can increase investment. We can try to encourage greater facilities to meet tomorrow's demands. Already we see across Canada new hotels and convention centres being built. There are special attractions going up, special visitors' services are transforming every area of the country and creating an even more exciting atmosphere.
For example, if I may just illustrate some of the areas in which we see new growth, there is in St. John's the new Hotel Newfoundland, which is a joint venture by Canadian National and private enterprise. Hilton International is expanding across the country with properties in Winnipeg, Hamilton, Charlottetown and Windsor. Here in the nation's capital we see three new hotels. Montreal has a new 825-room Sheraton centre. New hotels are planned for Saskatoon, Regina, and in Banff National Park, Alberta, two hotels and a 200-bed hostel. Many major hotel chains are undergoing renovation of existing properties. For example, Delta's Chelsea Inn in Toronto is now undergoing a 600-room expansion. The King Edward Hotel, long a well-known landmark in Toronto, has just gone through a magnificent restoration in the finest European tradition. In all, over $500 million in renovation, expansion and development of new hotels has been created across the country. New restaurants are springing up, catering to every taste and budget, not only in the first-class hotels but on an individual basis as well.
Canada certainly has a reputation for fine foods. Our chefs have proven that by winning top awards at many international culinary competitions. Coupled with that, we cannot overlook the fact that our cities are safe. This is one of the main areas of attraction. When people come to our country, especially from the United States, they marvel at the fact that they can walk on our streets feeling that they are very safe and will not be set upon or attacked by anyone. That has helped our tourist industry to a great deal. We must continue to preserve that type of atmosphere. I think it will attract a larger share of the lucrative market that is out there.

April 14, 1983

As I mentioned, convention facilities are in the process of being built in something like 12 of Canada's major cities, with a price tag of over $450 million. In Ottawa we know that the Rideau Centre will change the face of the downtown core. The project includes a hotel, theatres and shops to complement the new convention facilities.
Canada, I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, is on the threshold of change, not only in our cities, but in the wilderness areas as well. Our parks are among the most magnificent in the world. They are being developed year-round in various recreational programs. We know that we really have a wonderful land of recreational facilities in our natural resources of lakes, woods and forests of which many people from all over the world avail themselves. Wilderness retreats and resorts are expanding to meet the growing demands for the outdoors, both winter and summer. Time-sharing is becoming an increasingly popular leisure investment alternative, so that now vacationers can purchase time accommodation and lifestyle of their choice from a variety of prestige resorts across the country.
Let us go out to the West Coast for a moment. In British Columbia, Whistler and Blackcomb Mountains, two hours north of Vancouver, are being transformed into one of the largest resorts in North America, able to handle nearly 13,000 skiers a day. Combined with first-class convention facilities, accommodation and food outlets, Whistler will be a world-class resort.
More than $550 million is being spent on Panorama in B.C.'s Purcell Mountains and at Big White Ski Village in Kelowna. In Quebec, and here in Ontario, $120 million is budgeted to upgrade and expand the facilities of Mont Trem-blant, Mont Ste. Marie and Blue Mountain. These are just some of the resorts already under development. I am sure that tomorrow we will see others created from coast to coast.
Then we have the multiple special attractions. At a cost of $100 million, private industry has just completed Canada's Wonderland just north of Toronto. In Niagara Falls, Ontario, Marineland is undergoing a $75 million expansion which will include a monorail and a midway. With an investment of $415 million, Calgary is now preparing for the 1988 Winter Olympics, while Edmonton will host the World University Games this year.
I suggest that the Canadian tourism industry is also keeping pace with the latest development in technology. Telidon, which has been developed by the federal Department of Communications, will give consumers access to travel information 24 hours a day. Travel Canada, a computerized booking service between world tour operators and Canadian tourist facilities, will handle bookings and all negotiations at no cost. This makes Canada accessible as well as shows a commitment on the part
not only of the private investors, private operators, but certainly of the Provinces and of the federal Government as well.
More than $40 million is being spent to upgrade eight international airports in our country, and over $120 million on 11 national airports. Air Canada and CP Air are spending more than $800 million on Boeing 767s, the newest generation of fuel-efficient jet aircraft. VIA Rail is upgrading equipment and facilities to the tune of $100 million. The new ferry between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island will double the carrying capacity next summer.
Major developments are enhancing Canadian tourism from coast to coast and, I think we would have to agree, offering not only Canadian citizens, but also those from countries around the world, a multitude of great adventure vacation opportunities.
As I am sure Hon. Members opposite have suggested today, I think that much more can certainly be done and should be done. The Government of Canada, through support programs, in trying to help private investors through advertising, through promotion, through public awareness campaigns, and also providing free information facilities to tourist operators to let them know of Government programs of assistance which are available to them in various areas across the country, has shown a definite commitment to support and promote the Canadian tourist industry.

Mr. Speaker, since the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) spoke of the upgrading which is going on with VIA Rail, would he tell us just what sort of upgrading, if any, is occurring on the route through Jasper, which just recently, about a year and a half ago, lost its rail service and therefore cut off many Japanese and other tourists from across North America from that market? Has he any information as to what has happened with the VIA Rail service there? Is that one of the areas which will be upgraded, and can rail service of Jasper be expected to return to its old state or to be upgraded?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning the matter as to whether that service will be restored, it is perhaps a question which must be addressed to the Minister of Transport, (Mr. Pepin). However, when I referred to the upgrading of VIA Rail facilities, I was referring to the entire country, not only to this one particular area. I think we realize that VIA Rail, certainly in many parts of the country, is upgrading its service by way of new rolling stock, new equipment. We know of the new passenger trains which are running now in many parts of the country. This is certainly creating added facilities and will mean a greater attraction for tourists travelling across the country.
I have no information as to whether or not that particular service will be restored. I think that is something for the Department of Transport to consider.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gass:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of the Canadian tourist industry and calls upon the Government to recognize this industry as a major generator of employment, new economic growth, and foreign exchange, and that the Government accept its responsibility to increase the visibility of Canadian tourism, both at home and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure this afternoon to be able to take part in this debate on the motion put forth by the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) which, amongst other things, calls upon the Government to recognize the tourist industry as a major generator of employment, new economic growth, and foreign exchange and that the Government accept its responsibility to increase the visibility of Canadian tourism both at home and abroad.
There is little doubt in the minds of most people who are involved in the tourist industry, which is the second largest industry in this nation, that the Government could indeed be spending much more time planning and preparing for the implementation of a reasonable and respectable tourism industry policy across the country.
The Hon. Member for Malpeque has very ably pointed out, as have other speakers in the House today, many areas where the Government might produce a better climate under which we would see a greater number of tourist dollars coming into the country both from within and from abroad. speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: The first.

The Hon. Member states that it is the first. I can only take that as an indication that at the first opportunity he has to meet with his caucus colleagues he will advocate the Government's establishment of Tourism Canada as was mentioned earlier. Unless there is an election, hopefully we will see him in charge of the most deserving Department to be.
I intend to spend the short time that is available to me this afternoon discussing tourism in Canada's picture Province, the Province of New Brunswick. Indeed, tourism is the third largest industry in New Brunswick and it is extremely vital. It is probably a little known fact even to New Brunswickers that tourism is that important to the economy of that Province. In 1982 we saw some S350 million generated in revenue directly from the tourist industry. It is a major employer because in 1982 it created some 12,600 man-years directly and approximately 13,500 man-years in indirect employment. That is certainly not an insignificant amount. Since these people were drawing salaries and paying income tax, and the establishments that they were working for were receiving revenues from outside the Province and the country in many instances, a fair amount of money has been realized by the federal Government as well.
I want to refer to some of the remarks that were made by the former speaker, the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt), particularly those which have already been addressed by my hon. friend from the NDP, that is, with respect to his comment that VIA Rail has been upgrading facilities. It is interesting to note that the majority of tourists, some 91 per cent, who have been travelling to the Province of New Brunswick during the past year, have come by automobile. Of course they must purchase gas in order to travel, and they are faced, as we all are, with the unrealistic cost of gasoline in this nation, which is a direct result of an unrealistic taxation policy that was certainly implemented by a Government which gave no intention of doing so when it was asking Canadians to place their confidence in it during the last election.
Be that as it may, the point I wanted to make is that the Hon. Member for London West made reference to VIA Rail's upgrading of facilities. I wonder if he is aware that as far as New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and parts of Quebec are concerned, the Government's apparent view of upgrading a railway facility is to remove it. For example, the Atlantic

April 14, 1983

Limited has been removed. It was the most popular run in Atlantic Canada and had one of the highest user rates in the entire country. Indeed, it served the needs of the people of southern New Brunswick as no other public mode of transportation has or will in the foreseeable future, until such time as that train is restored to its proper place which I am confident will happen after the election of the Progressive Conservative Government, which I am looking forward to in the near future.
I would suggest that the trains that have been substituted locally for the Atlantic Limited are totally inadequate. Certainly no tourist or local resident can now be encouraged to travel through the southern part of New Brunswick, or indeed to and from the northern section of the Province, for recreational purposes because not only is the timing poor, the train often runs at capacity and, on other occasions, beyond standing room only. That is an indication of the importance of that rail service.
I would also be extremely remiss if I did not draw to the attention of the House the fact that 1983 will be the two hundredth anniversary of the Loyalist landing in New Brunswick at the port City of Saint John. It will be a marvellous occasion and celebration. We certainly look forward to an active participation by our fellow Canadians and hopefully from a great many visitors from the United States and abroad.
Many events will take place in the port City of Saint John. For instance, there will be a re-enactment of the Loyalist landing, various youth rallies, parades and blessings of the fleet. June 17 will be a very special and happy occasion at which time the Prince and Princess of Wales will be visiting the port City. I am pleased to say that during that time they will also be visiting my constituency of Fundy-Royal.
Another celebration will occur in 1984 in New Brunswick. It is the bicentennial anniversary. Many communities throughout the Province will be conducting their own bicentennial projects, and it should prove to be of a great deal of interest. Hopefully that will draw many tourists as well.
The year 1985 will be the two hundredth anniversary of the incorporation of the City of Saint John. I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that Saint John is Canada's oldest incorporated city, but for the benefit of the rest of those sitting in the House, I pass that information along. I know that you will want to convey to the residents of Saint John every good wish on their two hundredth anniversary in 1985. Of course, during that time we will be having the Summer Games in Saint John which will be a very exciting time for us.
I would like to speak briefly of the facilities available to tourists in southern New Brunswick. The St. John River system is one of the most beautiful river systems in the world, as well as its many tributaries, including the Belle Isle, the Kennebecasis, the Washadamock, the Grand Lake, the Jemseg and the Salmon River, and many other rivers which flow into the St. John River or through its system. It is rightfully known throughout the world as the Rhine of North America. We have over 460 miles of navigable water in the St. John River
system. I invite anyone who is a boating enthusiast to take advantage of that river system.
We have a series of wharves. I know that wharves do not fall under the purview of the Minister. Wharves comes under the purview of the Small Craft Harbours Directorate in the Department of Fisheries. I am delighted to see the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry here in the House this afternoon. Perhaps I can depend upon her to put in a good word with her caucus colleagues for some upgrading of the wharf system. I have been after the federal Government now for the last several years to spend some money on the wharves so that boaters, particularly from the United States, who come up in large fleets from time to time are able to dock. A great number came last year. The cruising club of America was in the St. John River system. Their fleet was a beautiful sight to behold. Members of the club spent some time on the river. Unfortunately the wharves, about which I have been talking to the Department of Fisheries for some time, were not in the best condition. The system did receive some money last year, for which I was grateful. I know the visitors and boaters to our area were grateful to have some small repairs done, but a great deal more attention could be paid to this situation.
I want to talk now about my own constituency and in particular, about Fundy National Park. A year ago last June I brought to the Government's attention, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, the fact that Fundy National Park exists. It is located in New Brunswick. I see the Minister responsible for parks is here in the House. I welcome him to this debate in the House of Commons this afternoon. I bring to his attention now that Fundy National Park does exist in New Brunswick, in the constituency of Fundy-Royal. This fact had gone unnoticed for a number of years by the federal Government. An advertisement in 1978 placed in the Reader's Digest stated that Fundy National Park was located in Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia is our sister Province across the Bay of Fundy. I am sure that all Nova Scotians would be delighted to have Fundy National Park in their Province. But it is located in New Brunswick. I want to clarify that point.
It was brought to my attention a year ago last June that the Government had finally resolved the difficulties with Fundy National Park's location. At that time the Government inserted another advertisement in the Reader's Digest concerning our national parks, and Fundy National Park was deleted altogether. Despite the fact that Fundy National Park was first misplaced by this Government in Nova Scotia and subsequently deleted altogether from Government advertisements, the park remains in New Brunswick. I understand the Government will open the gates this summer, and I hope the Government will be a little more positive in the future about Fundy National Park.
I have a few suggestions for the federal Government which deal with Fundy National Park. I hope the Government will take Fundy National Park into consideration in its upcoming budget. I hope the Minister responsible for Tourism will take
April 14, 1983

this subject under his wing and perhaps encourage his counterparts to allocate some more funding to encourage tourists to come to Canada, to New Brunswick, Fundy Royal and to Fundy National Park. I believe, and many other people believe, that this park is one of the most beautiful in Canada. Perhaps even the Minister would like to visit my constituency. I would be delighted to take them on a tour of the area.
Nevertheless, there are a good many things that bother us in New Brunswick about the Government's attitude toward Fundy National Park, not the least of which is an advertising program. Not very much has been done in the line of advertising over the past number of years for Fundy National Park. We would like to see the federal Government put some emphasis on the unique aspects of Fundy National Park. The highest tides in the world occur in the Bay of Fundy. Emphasis also should be placed on the flora and fauna of the area. The Government should be putting out brochures explaining the park and all of the things that are available and what a beautiful place it is.
I notice with some interest the budget of Fundy National Park seems to be falling behind in comparison to the moneys being allotted to Kouchibouguac Park which is in the constituency of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc), the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. I would like the Government to address the inequity of an entrance fee. There is a charge for Fundy National Park but not for Kouchibouguac Park.
We would like the facilities in Fundy National Park to be upgraded. We would like to see facilities for trailers increased. We believe the number of senior citizens travelling with trailers now is increasing. We should be providing more facilities in addition to those already in existence in the park. I might add that the trailer sites are always filled and there would be no problem filling more. We would like to see the Government improve and upgrade the swimming pool facility. There are not many parks in Canada that have a swimming pool. Fundy National Park does. This swimming pool draws its water from the Bay of Fundy. That is a unique situation. The water is heated, but because of changeable weather conditions it has limited usage. If the pool were enclosed this would be a definite asset.
We have a beautiful golf course which was originally intended to be an 18-hole golf course. It was built in 1948 and has nine holes. Although the original intention was for an 18-hole golf course, there has been no move since then to extend it from 9 holes to 18 holes.
There was a craft school in Fundy National Park. We would like to see that revitalized. It was supported and financed by the provincial Government. We would like to see some federal participation in that area.
Children's programs are something that should be addressed. I have some suggestions for some new facilities which might include such things as a maple sugar operation, a sawmill, a museum, and an original homestead modelled on one of the old homes there at the time of the takeover. A fishway should be built at Pointe Wolfe to improve salmon fishing facilities.
