There are many things we can do in the area of physical activities which promote health. I am thinking of trails for jogging, cross-country skiing and other activities which come to mind for Fundy National Park.
In closing I should like to say that the Province of New Brunswick should be commended for the work it has done in the past as far as promotion of salmon fishing, which is second to none anywhere in sports fishery, is concerned, and for the co-operation it has extended to the federal Department of Fisheries. It seems it has not been repaid in kind and now we are faced with some very ridiculous salmon fishing regulations which are not at all in the best interests of the sports salmon fishery in New Brunswick. I would like to see some attention paid to that industry as it is very important and very vital.
We have a great opportunity to exploit an area indigenous to New Brunswick in the Atlantic salmon sports fishery. We have some of the greatest salmon rivers in the world in the Province of New Brunswick. Certainly we would be unwise to continue on this course with reference to the sports salmon fishery in New Brunswick. I will have more to say about that at another time in another debate.
I support the motion of the Hon. Member for Malpeque. I look forward to a renewed and vigorous revitalization of the tourist industry, the tourist platform and the tourist Department by the federal Government under the auspices of an able and capable Minister who will give it every consideration. We look forward to grand and wonderful things in the department of the industry through the efforts of our tourism critic and his co-operation with the Minister who is now responsible for tourism in Canada and who should have a sole Ministry to administer under that portfolio.

Mr. Speaker, ours is a large country. It offers travellers, both Canadians and foreign, the widest choices in meeting their interests. Our cities have museums, art galleries, theatres and restaurants which are of world class. They offer those interested opportunities to watch the best in athletic competition, whether it be baseball, football or hockey, just to mention a few. Away from our cities we have scenery, mountains, rivers, lakes, forests, wilderness areas and wildlife the equal of any country or continent in the world.
People from all parts of the world should be flocking to Canada. Canadians should be visiting areas in Canada away from their homes. If we commissioned a study, I am sure we would find that very few people from Atlantic Canada have visited the Pacific Coast, that very few people from Winnipeg have been to Halifax or Saint John, and even fewer have been to Newfoundland. Most Canadians live in a belt 100 miles north of the American border. When they travel, they do not visit other parts of Canada. They go to Florida, Hawaii, Mexico, England, France and the Scandinavian countries. We ought to ask ourselves why they are doing this.

April 14, 1983
Supply
Canadians, especially those who do not live in British Columbia, know that the main reason for getting away from Canada is our winters. Canadians like to take winter holidays and get away to warmer climates, whether it be in the southern United States or in places like Hawaii. There is another important reason. It is the same reason that many non-Canadians do not come to Canada. It is because in Canada we have not worked out the kind of arrangements or package deals which are available in other countries. If Canadians want to take their holidays in Florida, Hawaii, England, France or any other country, they can usually work out a package deal which includes not only air fare but hotel accommodations.
Recently I had my office contact a travel agency here in Ottawa. We were told that we could obtain a package tour to fly from Montreal to Miami, Florida, and stay there for a week at a price of between $400 and $500 per person. This included the air face and hotel accommodation. Or we could take the same trip and stay for two weeks at a price of between $600 and $800 per person. We have nothing in Canada to match that.
In recent years our airlines finally realized that if they wanted to tap the big market, the people who were travelling but not in Canada, they would have to offer cheaper air fares. If one flies from Ottawa to Vancouver or from Halifax to Toronto, it is still necessary, even if one obtains cheap air fare, to pay $50 to $100 per day for a decent hotel. If we compare that with the deals one could make to travel to Florida, Hawaii or London, England, we see why Canadians and non-Canadians are not travelling in Canada and taking advantage of the facilities and the scenery available here. It is for this reason that many people flock to other countries.
Many countries in the world, both the industrialized and less developed ones, have recognized the benefits derived from promoting the tourist industry. The industry provides employment for large numbers of people. These jobs can and should be of a permanent nature. Unlike manufacturing industries which have gone into decline and the high technology industries we hope to encourage, both of which are highly capitalintensive, the tourist industry is labour-intensive. It should employ even more people. It will not become obsolete if it is modernized. It should be non-polluting. It should be promoted in ways it has not been promoted up to now.
Of course, the federal and provincial Governments have spent money on advertising to tell Canadians and other people about Canada's great scenery and events which take place such as concerts, ballets, folk festivals and multicultural events in various parts of Canada. Until the federal and provincial Governments get together with the transportation industry, with the hotel and motel groups and with restaurant groups in ways they have not already done, we will not succeed in convincing travellers, whether they be Canadians or foreigners, that they are as welcome in Canada and can obtain the kind of enjoyment when they travel here as they do in other countries.
To a large extent tourist industry facilities are operated by Canadians in small individually-owned operations. They have been very seriously and adversely affected by the recession. Business is down because people do not have money. When there are 1.5 million people unemployed, they will not travel to
the same extent as they did in other years, nor do they have money even if they do travel to spend like they used to. Business is down and the high interest rates to which the tourist industry and other industries have been subjected in recent years have driven many people in that industry, particularly small independent operators, whether they own a motel, hotel, restaurant, fishing facility or campsite, into bankruptcy or close to bankruptcy. They need to upgrade their facilities. They need money to continue to operate until the economy improves. What do they find? They find that the banks, having overextended themselves in loans to some of Canada's largest corporations, now have over $4 billion in noncurrent loans. That means that companies are not even paying the interest, let alone the principal which they borrowed from the bank. They find that the banks, having been burned by their mistaken loans to many of Canada's largest corporations, have been getting more and more tough with the small businessmen. Most operators in the tourist industry can be included in that.
Over 80,000 Canadian small businesses closed their doors in 1982, according to the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen. Among them were tourist operators. While this tragedy continues, the Canadian dollar is a bargain to foreign tourists, yet the Government is reluctant to advertise the tourist virtues of this great country in other but the most perfunctory way.
This same Government decries the fact that the national economy has been dragged into recession by the forces of the international market. We know that, along with everybody else, the small business sector has suffered. A large percentage of the 700,000 to 800,000 jobs that have been lost to the economy through lay-offs and shutdowns have been in the small business area. The coming summer period should provide an excellent opportunity for the tourist industry to attempt to recoup some of the jobs, but it needs a real program of support for its facilities. International tourism could be attracted to this country if the Government could work with the industry to provide support.
Earlier this week the Minister pointed with pride to the fact that 62 per cent of the applicants for the small business investment grants were farmers and fishermen. It is good to hear that, but it is strange that the same Minister who is responsible for tourism does not realize that his program missed the mark. These are the figures for small business loans. If the majority of the loans have been made to farmers and fishermen, it is obvious there has been very little assistance to the tourist industry.

800,000	fewer jobs than in 1981, it is time that this Minister rethought his strategy and started to provide Canadian small business with some access to working capital to improve and refurbish these facilities. He should begin today by participating with provincial Governments, municipal Governments, the

tourist industry and the provincial industry in rethinking policies to develop ways of pursuading Canadians and others to travel in Canada rather then outside Canada as has been done so frequently in the past.

Mr. Speaker, representing as I do one of the outstanding tourist areas of Canada, I commend the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) on the motion he has presented to the House today. The motion reads:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of the Canadian tourist industry and calls upon the Government to recognize this industry as a major generator of employment, new economic growth, and foreign exchange and that the Government accept its responsibility to increase the visibility of Canadian tourism both at home and abroad.
I want to deal with some of the major thoughts in connection with tourism from the federal angle. Today most provincial Governments spend large sums of money on tourism. They have Tourist Departments. Along with the municipalities, they are doing the job, but they receive very little assistance or encouragement from the Canadian Government.
Tourism is not recognized by the federal Government as an industry, but more or less as a promotion. It employs a large number of people and should be recognized as an industry. Until it is, it will not get its proper share of attention. It is a small business.
All of the Bills dealing with small business should be applicable to our campgrounds, motels and to those who provide any tourism service which makes the visit of people to this country more enjoyable. Until that is done, those trying to build up the tourism industry in this country will not get their full share. The Bill passed the other day in connection with the 4 per cent interest assistance for loans could be of tremendous advantage to the owner of some of our campgrounds who are having to pay high rates of interest. Even though they operate and are taxed as a business, they are not recognized as an industry by the federal Government. I would like the Minister to ensure that tourism does become an industry in this country.
There are no tax incentives for the tourist industry, none at all. Those who help bring thousands of visitors to this country, resulting in the spending of millions of dollars, should receive some tax incentives the same as those who drill for oil and dig for coal, as well as the many other activities in this country which produce wealth.
Tourism produces wealth for this country and, for the most part, takes nothing away other than souvenirs on which millions of dollars are spent. This adds to our foreign exchange. Visitors look at our beautiful mountains, hills, badlands, dinosaurs and whatever else a Province has to offer, and they enjoy it. All they take away is a beautiful memory of a beautiful country. However, no tax incentives are provided for this industry. There should be tax incentives for businesses catering to the tourist industry as with any other business in this country.
How many times do we hear talk about the "Dirty Spoon Cafe"? If there are such places, it is because there are no incentives or encouragements for them.
Supply
There is an association in western Canada called the Yel-lowhead Route Association. The route runs from Winnipeg to Brandon, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Lloydminister, Edmonton on to Vancouver or Prince Rupert, B.C., depending on which route you take. That organization has advanced the necessity for good tourist facilities. It has encouraged people to open good restaurants, serve good meals and maintain the beauty around campgrounds. All this is paying off. Many people now travel the Yellowhead route to Vancouver. This route has the lowest grade through the Rockies and the lowest snow fall. Tourist operators need tax incentives as an encouragement, particularly when they are contributing to the finances of the nation by attracting people back to this country.
Every time a tourist is disgruntled or frustrated and goes home angry, it is not likely he will return. Many of his friends will decide not to come either. Tourists must be kept happy if the industry is to grow, so more consideration must be given to public relations.
There are many restrictions on development, Mr. Speaker. In this country it is difficult to invest in a business. There are municipal inspections, environmental inspections, provincial inspections of utilities, planning board inspections, sewage disposal inspections-just one inspection after another. People become so frustrated that instead of investing in the industry they buy a Canada Savings Bond or put their money in the bank in order to avoid the hassle. Sometimes it is almost impossible to invest money because of Government restrictions. Some people claim that free enterprise does not work, but it is the shackles placed around it by the Government that make things difficult. It is very important to have proper facilities if people are to be encouraged to come to Canada, but at the present time too much red tape is involved.
I am glad that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is in the House as I want to deal with a case that he knows very well involving the Fleishman Cup. In 1981 110 young people from eastern and western Canada attended a ski meet in eastern Canada and planned one for western Canada in 1982. Every room was booked for the event at beautiful Lake Louise. Suddenly the Park's superintendent announced that it was necessary to obtain the permission of the Minister because it was a national event. But it was not a national event, Mr. Speaker. There was no hassle when it was held in eastern Canada. Just two weeks before the event, when all the arrangements were made and thousands of dollars had been spent, this is what happened. The event was not going to be attended by thousands of people but just by the parents of the skiers. These young people were likely to become Olympic competitors at some time. The competition is for the Fleishman Cup, previously called the Pontiac Cup, and it is held for amateur Canadian athletes between the ages of 15 and 20.
I telephoned the Minister's office and the secretary said that the event would not be accepted. I do not know how she knew that and I asked her to let the Minister decide. She said that it would not be accepted, that is all. I asked her to let it go to the

April 14, 1983
Supply
Minister at least. After several letters and two or three telephone conversations, the Minister said that in spite of all the inconvenience to people from eastern Canada, it could not be held. I asked him if it would do any harm to the snow, and he said, "It may". Mr. Speaker, it would not do any damage to the environment. The ski hills were there and the lifts were there. It was just a matter of red tape and letting some underling run the Department instead of the Minister.
This was not a national event but we could not persuade the Minister to change his mind, so 50 or 60 young people from eastern Canada will probably never go to Lake Louise again. They were so fed up after having made reservations and having a beautiful hill to ski on and then being told they could not go. It is not as if the resort was too busy either.
When I was teaching school there was a lad in grade four who was subnormal. Apparently there was a sheet of ice on his father's land and the other youngsters in the school yard were talking about going over there. He told them to go to another farm saying, "I don't want you to wear out our ice". I explained to him that you do not wear out ice, you enjoy it. Eventually the hockey game was held on that ice. That was the attitude of the Department of the Environment in this instance. It was as if these young people were going to wear out the snow.
We import chairs for ski lifts, Mr. Speaker, because they are not manufactured in Canada, but the importers do not receive a tax exemption. These ski lifts bring people to Canada and that helps our exchange and makes our community more buoyant, but no assistance is given for customs duties. There is assistance for many things but not for chairs for lifts. People are frustrated and discouraged. The red tape is worse in the national parks than anywhere else in Canada.
Every Province has its own unique beauty and attraction. I have been in all Provinces and the Territories and there is something for everyone in them all. I have enjoyed trips to the Arctic, the Maritimes, Newfoundland, Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. I have enjoyed the wheat lands of Saskatchewan even though I live in a wheat land area. I have enjoyed the beautiful scenery of the oceans and mountains of British Columbia. When people come to Alberta, they have a chance to see the majestic Canadian Rockies which are more beautiful than anything on the continent. I go there often because they are in my constituency, and I never fail to be inspired by the majesty of those mountains and have a greater appreciation of the omnipotent God who created them.
A man and his wife in the Banff area own a cottage which they purchased from the CPR in the red earth district beside Shadow Lake. It is a beautiful spot and I hope the Minister will go there if he has a chance. This family arranged for a bus to take handicapped people who could not walk very well to a point two miles from Shadow Lake so that they could then walk to the lake. Parks Canada wanted to close the area off. When I asked why, I was told they thought we did not need it. I wrote to the then Minister responsible for Parks, Mr. John Fraser. He was from Vancouver and he was good enough to come out and look at it. He said there was no reason to close it. At the meeting Hon. John Fraser told the park superintendent
that the road shall not be closed. It was not closed and it has not been closed since. It provides a wonderful holiday for people who cannot walk very well. It would not have bothered me as an individual if they had closed it. I walked the whole nine miles and enjoyed every step of the way. All around is one of the most beautiful scenes you could ever see, and the handicapped can enjoy it because a man is providing a chance to get there at reasonable cost. That is what we need to do with our tours. Let the handicapped come also. They do not take the mountains or the lakes away with them, but they do take away a tremendous memory and they want to come back again and again. I talked to a man in Calgary who was crippled and he told me he had gone to Shadow Lake every year for 15 years. He said, "Are you telling me I can't go anymore? That is cruelty." It was cruelty and, besides, we were killing an industry. However, it was not done, because that Minister used common sense in this matter and the Shadow Lake Route will remain open.
I am not going to say that the Province of Alberta is more beautiful than any other Province. I believe every Province has its own beauties. But I would like to outline some of the things we have in Alberta that you do not find elsewhere. My own home town, Drumheller, is nestled in the hills along the canyon of the Red Deer, as we call it, and the Red Deer River. People drive from Saskatchewan on Number 9 Highway through Drumheller, and almost every time I go by the Horseshoe Canyon I see 5 to 20 cars and trucks with Saskatchewan licence plates. They stop there to look at those badlands, that mass of little hills. They stop and the young people go up and down the hills and they enjoy it. And for those who have time to stay, there is a dinosaur trail. This is the place where the dinosaurs used to roam, and you can find their bones in the hills. As a boy I remember the Chamber of Commerce uncovering the bones of one of those huge monsters which weighed tons but had only a very small brain. When the vegetation changed through time they could not adjust their eating habits and so they died, and they are buried in the hills. The Chamber of Commerce uncovered the remains of one of these creatures, varnished the bones and left it in the hills. Tourists could see a dinosaur skeleton in the state in which it died. The trouble was, however, that everyone who came along wanted a souvenir, so they would take one of the bones, and it was not too long before our beautiful dinosaur had disappeared. Since that time, protection has been provided, and they are still there.
There is also the paleontology museum which is being established in that area by the provincial Government. It is going to bring scientists from all parts of the world into that beautiful Drumheller valley, the Canyon of the Red Deer. We have Lake Louise, one of the seven wonders of the world. We have Banff with all of its attractions. We have the foothills west of Longview and Kananaskis Park. All of these places draw people, and we should be encouraging people to build campgrounds, restaurants, motels. We should give them some

tax incentives and some help because they can bring people back and back again, and all they will take away is memories. They will eat our food, which will help the farming industry. They will buy our goods which helps the people who produce souvenirs. This is a tremendous opportunity-

Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) knows, tourism is important to me and to the people I represent in the constituency of South West Nova, as it is probably important to his own constituency. It has been interesting, Mr. Speaker, to hear how beautiful Canada is from sea to sea. There are many Canadians who have not had the opportunity to speak about the beautiful places there are to see here in Canada.
I welcome the topic of this Opposition day because I think for once we should sit down and think about the importance of tourism in Canada. I have learned, from listening to Hon. Members who have spoken here in the House, that they all have their own special area they want to talk about. That is realistic. It is also very isolating when it comes to the whole total picture of the role of Canada and the federal Government in tourism. It is interesting to note, when one looks at the figures, that more and more Canadians are travelling across Canada, whether it be expensively or cheaply. They are taking advantage of this great country called Canada and what it has to offer, not only to Canadians but to Canada's many visitors. It is perhaps quite natural for Canadians to take these areas for granted. However, once Canadians began to realize the importance of tourism to Canada, both for employment and as a source of revenue, they began to question the roles of Government in this industry, federal, provincial and municipal governments which benefit from the tourist industry. The Minister mentioned this morning that there were 40 federal Departments and agencies which have programs which support and advance the Canadian tourism industry, from Parks Canada to Fisheries and Oceans, to the youth exchange programs of the Secretary of State. Perhaps I might be a little parochial, since I am speaking as the Member for South West Nova, and say there is one agency which has taken a very active part in promoting tourism in the southern end of Nova Scotia, and that is the Crown Corporation CN Marine. CN Marine operates two facilities in the area. I read with pleasure a recent press release which reads as follows:
Cruise ship luxury and amenities will greet tourists travelling between Maine and Nova Scotia this spring when CN Marine introduces a new MV Bluenose to year-round service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor.
The 1,100-passenger ship which will provide the improved level of service is the newest addition to CN Marine's fleet, MV Jutlandica. She will be completely refitted for her new role and undergo a name change to maintain the tradition of "Bluenose" service.
I would add here, between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor, Maine. It goes on to say:
The Bar Harbor gateway to Nova Scotia was established 26 years ago by the original Bluenose auto ferry. During that time almost 2.5 million passengers have enjoyed the crossing of the Bay of Fundy and come to regard it as an enjoyable part of their vacation.
Supply
Upgrading this service will bring many more tourists to Nova Scotia. We have in the southern end of the Province two ports of entry for tourists, the ferry services and Air Canada. This is federal Government involvement. We have Parks Canada, the Kejimkujik Lodge. We have historic sites, Fort Anne and Fort Royal. These are all tourist attractions maintained by, as the Minister said, one of 40 federal Departments and agencies.
I was pleased as well to hear the Minister say he was seeking incremental funds for federal marketing of tourism, as well as pressing forward with regional development initiatives for tourism. We also know there have been regional development tourism packages between the federal Government and many Provinces, in particular Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, which have been very effective in creating interest in advancing tourism in Canada.
We have heard today, Mr. Speaker, that there should be federal tax incentives. I would like to point out to all Members of the House that the Provinces and municipalities also receive revenue. Perhaps they should be asked to provide tax incentives. What type of tax incentives are the Opposition Members talking about? Perhaps they should go back and talk to the Provinces. I would think that tourism is a much more local matter, and tax incentives might be looked at from the provincial level. They might look at liquor and food taxes, for example.
I have already mentioned that tourism is an essential element of economic activity in South West Nova. Each year thousands of American and Canadians enter Nova Scotia through the Ports of Yarmouth or Digby, or via Air Canada which has a direct service from Boston to Yarmouth. Perhaps Nova Scotia is lucky in that we have had a long-time connection with the eastern United States seaboard. We have welcomed visitors and tried to keep them here. Tourism is an important economic activity in Nova Scotia. Expenditures in 1981 by a total of almost 4.5 million resident and non-resident visitors to and within the Province totalled approximately $460 million. Where did the visitors come from? On an international basis we saw 40,861 visitors from overseas, and 325,016 from the United States, for a total of 365,877 visitors to Nova Scotia from outside the country. How much money did they leave behind? Forty-nine million dollars. On the other hand, non-resident Canadian visitors numbered 723,000, with provincial resident visitors totalling 3,295,000, for a total of
4,018,000	visitors. They left a total of $410 million in the Province. The total of international and Canadian visitors comes to 4,383,877, with a total expenditure of $459 million in the Province.
We must have been doing something right in the Province because I know for a fact that although tourism decreased considerably in some areas, Nova Scotia did not feel the great impact some areas did. Perhaps it is the beauty of Nova Scotia. Perhaps it is its accessability for those visitors. Our own people of Nova Scotia were travelling around the Province, which says it is a good place to visit.

April 14, 1983
Supply
The expenditures I mentioned produced an income to the tourist industry of $600 million, or 8.4 per cent of the gross provincial product. This makes tourism the sixth largest revenue earner in the Province. The 8.4 per cent in turn generated $62 million in tax revenues, which is about 3 per cent of total provincial Government revenue and .3 per cent of total Canadian Government revenue. It produced $25 million induced investment and 25,000 person years of employment. This tourism-related employment represents about 7.3 per cent of the provincial labour force. That means that the economic activity generated by tourism is important to Nova Scotia, and it is important that all levels of Government recognize that.
We heard earlier a Member talk about the Loyalist Days and the ongoing celebrations. Well, there has been a hive of activity in the southern end of the Province which I represent, and in other areas across the Province, on Loyalist Days. Activities to date have been very successful, and we are looking forward to them as they occur throughout the summer in the various communities. I might mention this means that tourists will be attracted to the area, and I hope these activities are successful. I know that many groups in heritage programs in the southern end of the Province have put a lot of time and effort into them, and they look forward to the approval of their visitors.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to spend a few minutes on the federal Government's direct involvement in Nova Scotia, in particular the Canada-Nova Scotia tourism industry development subsidiary agreement which was concluded at the end of March. The federal Government has been most actively involved in planning and programming the tourism industry in Nova Scotia through this agreement. The agreement evolved from a tourism development policy and strategy for Nova Scotia prepared back in August, 1976. The original duration of the agreement was from April, 1977 to March, 1982.
I remember when it was being developed. I know the time and effort put into that agreement by both the Province and the federal Government. There was an extension from March, 1982 to March of 1983 for a completion of commitments, and the Minister approved that extension. Therefore, all money committed under that program was used in Nova Scotia. What were the objectives of that agreement, Mr. Speaker? They were to create employment opportunities and increase incomes by increasing the length of the tourist season, increasing the total number of visitors, extending the length of stay, increasing the expenditures per traveller per day, and distributing travel expenditures geographically.
As a result, that agreement provided destination areas which include Annapolis Basin, Lunenburg, the eastern shore, Pictou County, Bras d'Or and Louisbourg. In my constituency the destination area was the Annapolis Basin, the funding for which was to create a major attraction in the Annapolis basin which would have international significance.
Under that five year agreement, $2,198,160 was spent in the Annapolis basin. What did it achieve? The Annapolis Royal Community, through its development commission, fully supported and implemented the tourism plan. The botanical
gardens, the restoration of the Adams-Ritchie House and Kings Theatre, streetscape improvement and the waterfront walkway project have all been undertaken in order to attract the tourists who are coming to Nova Scotia to stay longer and to visit and learn about the history of one of the oldest settlements in North America. I say that because we have the historic Habitation at Port Royal and the historic Fort Anne in Annapolis Royal, both being very old areas of the cradle of our history of the settlements which came to Canada.
The total funding under that agreement was budgeted at $13.75 million, based on an 80/20 cost-sharing formula. The federal Government, of course, picking up the 80 per cent, contributed $11 million and the provincial Government contributed $2.75 million.
I hope that in the future we will see a new agreement, a new program coming into play between the federal Government and the Province of Nova Scotia. No matter what shape or direction it takes, I am sure that having had the experience of the last six-year agreement, we have learned a lot. I will not presuppose what the Province is suggesting to the federal Government, but I do hope that the federal Government is listening and that there will be some destination and areas.
Before closing, I would again like to thank the Hon. Member for Malpeque who has allowed me to speak on tourism, such an important economic activity in the constituency of South West Nova. I would say to all Hon. Members opposite that anyone who would like to come and visit down in the southern end of Nova Scotia, the most southern area aside from the Niagara Peninsula, is most welcome to come.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to tell the Hon. Member who has just concluded his remarks that we are looking forward to visiting Nova Scotia, I hope. First of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) for enabling us today to debate a very interesting and very important subject, because it is widely acknowledged that the tourist industry ranks second in our economy. I also want to commend all Hon. Members who have spoken so far, because I have the impression today that the debate has been very constructive. Naturally, we have made some instances to the Government concerning the development of the tourist industry, which is very important in terms of investments and the number of jobs involved. I know for a fact that in the past three or four years inflation has hit that industry very hard, as it did so many others. Given its importance, we cannot miss the opportunity to urge the Government to review its legislation, to acknowledge the leading role of that sector, and to try to promote the industry in close co-operation with the provinces and various organizations. I believe it would be to our advantage to keep in close touch with the Tourism Industry Association of Canada which rightfully does not mince words now and again when it makes recommendations to the federal and provincial Governments.
April 14, 1983

As others have done, I want to take this opportunity to say that my province is interested indeed in promoting the tourist industry. And so does my riding, for even though all my colleagues may not come often to visit my riding, I could say that my friends opposite do visit my riding at certain times. Of course, they usually come at election time, Mr. Speaker, but I am sure they found some very interesting spots to visit. We also have some very good areas for hunting and fishing that could be developed. We have a wonderful museum in Joliette which is known nationally, and I think we have some pieces that compare very favourably with those in world famous museums. In Rawdon, near Joliette, more and more people are visiting Darwin Falls, which has been developed very satisfactorily for several years as a tourist attraction.
I would also like to draw the Government's attention to the fact that in Sainte-Marguerite, we have the Doncaster Indian Reserve. The reserve is under-utilized by the Indian Band. It covers six square miles and has beautiful lakes and hunting areas. I did make a number of recommendations a while ago, and I hope my comments will be considered with a view to making the reserve accessible to the general public and the surrounding municipalities, while of course respecting the rights of the Indians. Perhaps agreements could be concluded with the Indian Band, under which the general public could make use of the area and visitors from outside Quebec and outside the country could enjoy a few days of wonderful peace and quiet.
When we talk about the investment or funding required to build up the tourist industry, and we realize that $400 billion is spent directly or indirectly throughout the world, and that $15 or $17 billion in Canada creates one million jobs, and that $7 billion goes to National Revenue I think it is quite interesting to consider this question, especially in Quebec where we are talking about $900 million for the tourist industry which will create 100,000 jobs. I think we are entitled to ask the Government for this kind of help, especially in the present situation, where it is not easy to maintain a number of industries. However, there is no doubt in my mind that trade and industry deserve our special attention.
There are three basic principles we should remember. One is to try and keep Canadians inside Canada. I feel it is important to encourage Canadians to visit Canada and to visit other provinces, so that we can learn to know each other and again a better understanding of each other's needs and aspirations. We must also consider how we can attract larger numbers of visitors to Canada to enjoy the natural wonders this country has to offer. We should also concentrate on ways of getting people to prolong their stay in Canada.
These three concepts are very important, and I know that nothing will happen unless we do something about it, and I think, as others have said before me, that we should enter into
Supply
agreements with the provinces. We should also know how to handle their priorities in a spirit of honest cooperation. I feel that we should work together with the Canadian Tourist Association and other associations that promote tourism. There are all kinds of activities that come to mind. Montreal has the Expos and the Canadiens, Quebec City has the Nor-diques, and they attract people from outside the country. However, I think the Government should try to play a coordinating role with respect to this industry which is extremely important to our economy. As far as my own province is concerned, I am aware that agreements do exist, under which the Province of Quebec can get a financial contribution on a 60-40 basis-60 per cent from the Federal Government-for projects submitted by the Province to the Federal Government. This is being done elsewhere, there is no doubt about that, and I want to congratulate the Government on taking this approach. I think we should continue the good work, considering the importance of this industry, not only financially but also from the employment point of view. There is no doubt that our country is extremely interesting to visit; we could probably do even more to promote our tourist attractions and the dual character and diversity of Canada which millions of visitors to our country find interesting and of which we are aware ourselves, but even so, I believe that we should probably think about encouraging Canadians to travel throughout the country, for instance by providing certain tax cuts.
I believe that the possibility of offering certain benefits to Canadians who visit another province could be seriously considered. We could also think about implementing a policy to reduce transport costs between provinces. I am aware that the country is facing enormous deficits, but in view of the tax revenue produced by this industry, I believe that a serious evaluation would show that every dollar invested in the tourism industry could bring many more.
I would not want to omit to mention the efforts made by the Government to promote convention centres and the hotel industry. We all know that our Canadian cities have an increasing number of hotels sufficiently modern and well-organized to accommodate guests. However, it is one thing to have the hotels and convention centres required, but it is another to see that they are booked and used.
Mr. Speaker, I know that others will want to speak after me, but I would like to make a few comments about the importance of this industry. In view of the present situation, I believe that the Government, the Minister and the Members on the other side can count on a loyal and objective Opposition if the Government decides to suggest something in keeping with the point of view that we defended today. Of course, we want our various provincial Governments to examine this issue. However, we would like the Federal Government to become even more readily involved in this industry and to discuss this issue with the provinces.

April 14, 1983
Supply
As for the Canadian Tourism Association's interesting suggestions, I feel that we need everyone, and of course this also means businessmen, to use all our potential and have all the benefits of a well-organized and well-structured tourism industry. This is my wish, and I am pleased to see that everyone in this House can make such objective comments today and that so many Members can show their interest in this industry, all of which, of course, aims at putting back our economy on the right track by every means available, at creating a certain number of jobs and maintaining those which now exist, as well as improving the state of our economy.
This debate provides an excellent opportunity to make suggestions and assure the Government that we are willing to cooperate with any initiative which would improve this industry and urge Canadians to visit their own country so that they will know it, defend it and serve it better, and at the same time, there is no doubt that if our foreign visitors sense a greater unity in Canada and are more aware of the sites to visit, they will use their vacation in Canada more profitably. Mr. Speaker, I hope that the comments of all my colleagues and the Members opposite, who have shown a lot of interest in this matter, will catch the attention of the Minister and that we shall be able to work together for a good case, namely the development of the Canadian tourism industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rene Cousineau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join all the previous speakers to congratulate the Hon. Member of the riding of Malpeque (Mr. Gass) on introducing this motion. I congratulate as well all those who took part in the debate today with a non-partisan approach and, I must say, in a very positive and very objective way, because all Canadians agree that the tourist industry plays an extremely significant role in the Canadian economy. It has been said that 1.1 million jobs are related to tourism and that one out of ten Canadians works in the tourist sector. I should think that we all agree that tourism is very important in Canada and that we must do our very best to make people feel that they are welcomed in Canada.
This morning, Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) (Mr. Rompkey) mentioned only a few of the many initiatives taken by this Government to support the tourist industry in Canada. Unfortunately, perhaps some Members cannot appreciate or are unaware of the extent of that support.
I am grateful for this opportunity to enlighten the Hon. Member for Malpeque and his colleagues on the initiatives of the Government and our successful efforts to support Canada's tourist industry. I should like to emphasize particularly the close co-operation between federal Government, the Provinces, the Territories and the private sector to develop that very important industry.
Ever since 1946, Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial ministers responsible for tourism have met every year to deal with major issues, to exchange ideas, to discuss matters of
serious concern and to act in consultation with one another. The officials at both levels of government have frequent meetings by themselves and with industry representatives to develop marketing plans and to co-ordinate their implementation throughout the world. Hon. Members who have taken part in international tourist events either overseas or in the United States are aware that the federal government is responsible for co-ordinating the activities of the various provinces and the private sector under the Canadian flag. The federal officials in charge of tourism are co-operating with their counterparts in the public and private sectors and setting up advertising and marketing programs in all parts of the world. These initiatives not only obtain marketing awards in international competitions, they are also an economical way to invest our taxpayers' money.
Hon. Members are certainly aware that since 1974, thanks to ancillary agreements on the expansion of the tourist industry, the federal government has invested, together with the provinces and the territories, over $220 million to expand and up-date tourist equipment and facilities. Without this financial assistance, such tourist attractions as those of Whistler Village in British Columbia, or Acadian Village in New Brunswick, would not exist today.
One realizes just how serious this Government has been about tourism in Canada when one discovers that it set up as early as 1978 a Consultative Task Force on Tourism. Made up of representatives of both management and labour, it advises the Government on ways and means to improve the performance of the industry. It has submitted many recommendations, most of which have been accepted and implemented by the federal authorities. If the Government is doing nothing to develop the tourist industry in Canada, as the motion now before us would have it, why then did the Minister of State (External Relations) (Mr. Lapointe), while he was Minister of State (Small Business and Tourism) come to launch in cooperation with provincial and territorial tourism authorities a national tourism program that included a series of individual programs setting forth the strategies and priorities of each participating Government for industrial growth and development?
If the Government is doing nothing to improve our tourist industry's competitive situation, what is to be made of the national program we launched in 1980 to foster the construction and expansion across Canada of international trade centres and convention centres by providing a total of nearly $200 million worth of support to nine major facilities? Let us recall the Canada Marketing Support Program launched in 1982 to help organizers develop all-inclusive travel plans to and within Canada? It is estimated that the program, with a $1 million funding, will generate this year $37 million in allinclusive travel plans within Canada.
April 14, 1983

Mr. Speaker, if the Government does not recognize or believe in the tourist industry, how is it that in September 1982 it did recognize and honour, on World Tourism Day, 20 Canadians from all across Canada who made significant contributions to the growth and expansion of the tourist industry? How is it that also in 1981, the Government allocated an additional $9 million over a three-year period to improve the marketing of Canada as a travel target?
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Small Business and Tourism) has already referred to some 40 federal Departments and agencies that have programs designed to influence and help the tourist industry. For example, the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (Mr. Munro) has recently reached with the Northwest Territories an agreement with a major component for the development of small business and tourism. A similar agreement is under consideration with the Yukon. My colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, (Mr. De Bane), who is here this afternoon, is implementing a small craft harbour program supplying pleasure boating services that are used each year by thousands of Canadians and visitors. The Minister of Environment (Mr. Roberts), who was in the House earlier, is much too modest to say so, but as Minister responsible for Parks Canada he knows that many of our national parks and historic sites have been designated as world heritage sites by Unesco.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government does not acknowledge that the tourist industry plays a major role in job creation, why do tourism projects account for such a large share of this Government's employment programs? The summer employment program for students, the new NEED Program, is of great assistance to employers in the tourist industry. In addition to that, we also have training programs for specialized workers in fields related to tourism which come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
My colleague the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) may have been too modest to refer to himself, so it is with pleasure that I mention the efforts he made on behalf of tourism when he was Minister of National Revenue. I am glad to point out to Hon. Members that it was he who launched a review of the customs program which will soon make it easier to hold international conventions in Canada. He is the one who undertook to set up duty-free shops at various ports of entry. He is the one who decided that Customs inspectors would provide visitors driving in from the United States with a tourist information booklet welcoming them into Canada. And since he became Minister responsible for Tourism, my colleague has decided to hold regular meetings with leaders of the Canadian Tourist Association, the national organization speaking for the industry, in order to obtain their views and advice on matters the Association feels are essential and advantageous to the growth and development of the industry.

This may be news to some Hon. Have Hon. Members heard of TOURCAN, the national market for Canadian buyers and sellers of tourist products? Do they realize that together those markets, operated by the Canadian Government Office of Tourism and supported by all the Provinces, Territories and the private sector, have generated will over S250 million in new tourist revenues for Canada since 1977?

Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House to the tourism industry in the National Capital region. I would like to point out how important it is for this region to recognize visitors to the Canadian capital, to have well-maintained roads and to insist on the participation and involvement of the provincial Governments.
I would also like to point out to the House that a recent study of the National Capital Commission stated that 2.5 million visitors came to Ottawa each year, 65 per cent of which were Canadians, which means that 1.6 million Canadians visit their capital. Of these, 70 per cent came to Ottawa by car, and the rest came by plane, bus or bicycle; 30 per cent or nearly
330,000	came from Quebec, more specifically from Montreal, the Eastern Townships, Quebec City, the North Shore or the Gaspe Peninsula, and 15 per cent of these 330,000 Quebec visitors to the capital region crossed the Ottawa river to visit Gatineau, Buckingham, Thurso or Hull.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, because here we have a number of people, very smart people for the most part, I believe, who took highway 417 near Rigaud on their way to Ottawa after having left Montreal through the Metropolitan Boulevard. When they needed gas, well, they simply bought some. I have nothing against people who sell gas along highway 417 but I would rather have seen them take highway 50 which is supposed to be completed in 4, 5, or ten years, and buy gas in my constituency, that is quite normal. Furthermore, it generates employment, and that is true also of restaurants. I mention that because we have forgotten lately about highway 50 and how important it is for Quebecers to travel and leave a

few dollars here and there in the various constituencies around Montreal as they head westward. I am not the only one to raise that issue. Even the strongest advocates of independance in the Outaouais region refer quite often to highway 50 which is vital to the economic development of that area.
I wanted that to be put on the record, Mr. Speaker, because in the Outaouais region, this issue is of the highest importance. In conclusion, I would like to thank again the Hon. Member for Malpeque who has given us the opportunity to let all Members know that the Government of Canada is deeply concerned with the tourist industry in the best interest of Canada and of all Canadians. I am satisfied that all Members are looking forward in 1984 to the 50th anniversary of the continuous support directed at the tourism industry by the federal Government.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great honour to speak on the Private Member's motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass). This motion is timely. I want to talk about the tourist industry, not only in the east but also in northern Ontario and particularly in the riding from which I come, that of Timiskaming.
I would like to take this opportunity today to express the concerns of many areas of Canada. The tourist industry should be an umbrella comprised of provincial and municipal Governments and individuals with the federal Government being the top part, co-ordinating that industry, whether it be in Newfoundland, British Columbia or Northern Ontario. We should ensure that we all work together in what has to be one of the most important small-business industries in Canada. Approximately 1.3 million individuals are employed seasonally across Canada in the tourist industry. This takes in students who have just graduated from high school, university students returning home for summer employment, trappers and fishermen who work during the summer months. The people of northern Ontario and in other parts of the country are concerned about energy-related problems and their effects on the tourist industry.
1 would like to make a few comments relating to the reliance of the tourist industry on the energy program. If we look back five years ago, we see that the costs of travelling, for example, from nothern Ontario to the Province of Alberta were relatively low, or if Albertans wanted to travel to northern Ontario or Prince Edward Island, the costs were likewise relatively low. When one went to fill up the gas tank it used to cost $15. Now we are looking at $30 or $35. That is one of the problems which is hurting the industry across Canada.
In my riding we rely upon people from the larger centres in southern Ontario to visit our small fishing camps that might have as many as four employees. I imagine there are Members on both sides of the House who certainly enjoy during the summer months (flying) into remote areas to fish for lake trout, speckled or whatever. At one time the cost of such a flying trip amounted to $75 to $100. Now we are looking at
$500 to $1,000 for the same trip. This is causing grave problems for the tourist industry because tourists are no longer coming.
Energy is a key part of the tourist industry across Canada, and people have expressed their concerns to me, and the Hon. Member for Timiskaming, in terms of interest rates, a very crucial problem affecting the survival of the industry. Most operators in northern Ontario rely upon a five or six-month period of time in order to make sufficient funds to carry them over the year. In the last two or three years the staggering costs of money they have been required to borrow in order to start up in the spring and to get in their supplies have affected their ability to survive. In the last year numerous small industries across the country which have tried to refinance, have ended up closing or have been put into a financial bind trying to operate their camps and to find extra employment to help offset their operational costs.
Another concern of Hon. Members on both sides of the House is the issue of acid rain. Acid rain has become a crucial consideration of tourism. For years and years fishermen were able to go into various lakes and catch speckled trout, lake trout and pickerel. The camps on such lakes relied on the literature they sent out each year showing the size of lake trout and various other fish. Those lakes are now in trouble, in grave trouble. When this happens, the industry on the lake is also in severe trouble. This is happening not only in northern Ontario but across the country.
I am pleased the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) sits on the Committee on Acid Rain because he knows the concerns of the tourist industry. This Committee has to work closely with this industry in an attempt to resolve the problem of acid rain. If we do not work strong and lobby hard in the years to come, the industry in northeastern Ontario and all across the country will be jeopardized. If we look at the various ministries of natural resources and their restocking programs, we see that year in and year out they stock lakes with fingerlings. I must say that these fingerlings do not reproduce. We are taking dollars and investing them back into the lakes. Until we resolve the problem of acid rain, the lake stock will not multiply and reach the levels of the past.
Over the last few months Air Canada has offered special rates for trips out of the country. I would like to see special rates being given for people to travel to my riding of Timiskaming from St. John's, Newfoundland or from Vancouver, British Columbia. I would like to see them provided with an opportunity to travel to my riding at a reduced rate rather than being faced with the outrageous costs of travelling via Air Canada to the area. It is very important for us to look at that and do our utmost in years to come.
Also in the area of transportation, I remind the House that we have the huge and beautiful Trans-Canada Highway which passes through my constituency. In years gone by people enjoyed towing their trailers across the country, visiting various communities. How many trailer manufacturers have

we lost over the years due to the rising cost of energy? I hope the budget which will be brought down next Tuesday will contain something to alleviate this problem. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) should do something for the tourist industry in terms of the cost of energy.
In closing I wish to say that I am very pleased to have had the opportunity to speak on a subject which I feel is important and has been often neglected. We must remember that at least 1.3 million people are employed in the tourist industry. Unless the federal Government, the provincial Governments, the municipalities and individual tourist operators start working together, we will be in trouble in years to come. We must provide the industry with some incentives, whether it be special bank interest rates for those who purchased resorts over the last five years or incentives in terms of the employment of students. In days of high unemployment we realize that people who would like to travel cannot do so because they are receiving Unemployment Insurance benefits or some social assistance.
It has been a great pleasure to participate in the last ten minutes of this important debate concerning tourism, and I thank my colleague for allowing me the opportunity to speak.

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER BE APPOINTED TO ENFORCE LEGISLATION

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on March 24 I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding the continuing violations of the Official Languages Act and asked that he appoint a Minister with special responsibilities to enforce the legislation in all Departments, agencies and Crown corporations.
My question was prompted by the recent report of the Official Languages Commissioner wherein he cited a number of examples of the law being ignored or contravened.
During the past year I have personally brought several cases to the attention of this House, the Government, and the Official Languages Commissioner. First, there was the case of the Old Port of Montreal, a federal agency which advertised entirely in French, even in the English language Montreal Gazette. Second, there were cases of English-speaking citizens in Montreal visiting their families at the federal penitentiaries at Laval, Quebec who were unable to get service in English at
Adjournment Debate
the gate and in some cases were refused entry. Third, there have been many Montrealers who have been unable to get Manpower retraining courses in English, and often other Manpower services in their own language. Fourth, there have been several examples in the past year of federal Government Departments putting up billboards entirely in French in districts of Montreal which are predominantly English.
The Official Languages Act requires the federal Government and all agencies to provide services in both official languages to the citizens of this country, and obviously that they be well prepared to do so in bilingual areas such as Montreal where there are large numbers of the official language minority.
Unfortunately, this is not being done, and in many cases there does not seem to be an understanding among the Civil Servants of their obligation to do so. Time and again, even in Ministers' offices in this city, I run into Civil Servants and staff who think that everything in Quebec should be in French and outside Quebec, bilingual. Even among some Ministers and Deputy Ministers, there is no political will to enforce the official bilingualism policy.
What I have described so far has taken place at the federal level, but it has taken place at a time in Quebec when there has been a provincial Government situation that is much worse. As Hon. Members know, Quebec Bill 101 has been very hard on English-speaking, bilingual and immigrant Quebecers. In some cases they have been forced into French-speaking schools. They have been forced to take down their English and bilingual signs. There are many places where they cannot get service in English at Quebec Government offices. I have many examples of senior citizens who cannot get any kind of service in their own language. These measures have been extremely coercive and oppressive.
The most recent scandal was the St. Mary's Hospital case where the Office de la Langue Fran?aise condemned the hospital because not all of its employees were able to speak French to certain patients. This was despite the fact that the hospital had a very good bilingual capacity and was very capable of providing services in French. Historically, this hospital was built by the English-speaking community in Montreal. What is particularly grating in this case is that approximately 50 per cent of the moneys for hospitalization and medicare in Quebec, as in all Provinces, comes from the federal Government.
On several occasions I have recommended that the federal Official Languages Act should apply to provincial institutions where there is substantial federal funding under joint federal-provincial funding agreements. At the present time the responsibility for enforcing the Official Languages Act is under the Deputy Ministers. Obviously this is not adequate. The Official Languages Commissioner can report violations and work with Departments to correct short-comings, but he has no administrative responsibility. The Prime Minister must assign a Minister who will have the responsibility of enforcing the Official Languages Act in all areas of the federal Government.

April 14, 1983
Adjournment Debate
If a good law is to have credibility, and I think the Official Languages Act is a good law, it must be enforced. In addition, the time has come for amendments to that Act. At the present time a Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons is discussing such amendments to improve the law, bring it up to date and make it more just for all Canadians, both English and French speaking.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER BE APPOINTED TO ENFORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine-East (Mr. Allmand) for his concern regarding the application of the Official Languages Act. I would like to point out that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who is the Minister responsible for the application of the Official Languages Act, meets annually with his officials to evaluate the annual report submitted by the Commissioner of Official Languages. The Act has been in existence for ten years, and although much progress has been made during the past decade, the Government realizes that much remains to be done, although we should be careful in our evaluation of the Official Languages policy. The important thing is to ensure that Crown corporations and federal agencies and departments observe not only the spirit but also the letter of the Act. This is very important. In his last report, the Commissioner of Official Languages pointed out, in referring to Air Canada, that a great deal of work had been accomplished during the past ten years, but it was also true that although Air Canada continued on its expedition to the Official Languages summit, a lack of qualified climbers was still impeding the final phase of the ascent.
Nevertheless, I would like to give the Hon. Member the assurance that the Government is following very closely what is happening to the practical application of the Official Languages Act, and that at the present time, considering the projects that have been realized, the Government entirely approves of the fact that the President of the Treasury Board should be responsible for the application of the Act. However, if other points were brought to the attention of the House, perhaps some other action would be taken. Before finishing my comments, I would like to point out that between the 1981 and the 1982 reports, the Commissioner of Official Languages noted a drop of 20 per cent in the number of complaints regarding the application of the Official Languages Act. This means that Canadians have learned to live with the Official Languages Act but that we must remain vigilant to ensure that the basic rights of both French and English Canadians are respected throughout the country.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-TREATMENT OF INCOME DERIVED THROUGH SERVICE TIPS. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ACTION
INCOME TAX-TREATMENT OF INCOME DERIVED THROUGH SERVICE TIPS. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 9 I rose in the House to put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) concerning what seemed to me then, as it does now, to be a very unfair
policy regarding the tips given to waiters and waitresses in the country. The problem arises from the dual standard that seems to have been set by the Government on these tips. They must be claimed as income by those who receive them and therefore are included in taxable income.
The other side of the dual standard is that the waiters and waitresses cannot claim benefits on that total income. They are taxed on the larger amount which includes the tips but the benefits are provided according to the lesser amount. They are not allowed to include the tips for unemployment insurance, Canada Pension Plan, Quebec Pension Plan, Workman's Compensation, and in fact holiday pay could be brought into this as well. If they are taxed on the income which includes tips or gratuities, they should also be entitled to the social benefits according to that income.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that this affects some 200,000 workers across Canada, I understand some 85,000 workers alone in the Province of Quebec. These are workers who are difficult to organize or unionize because of the high turnover in their occupations. I was asking the Minister to take some action to rectify this apparent inequity or dual standard which the Government has chosen to place upon waiters and waitresses.
I believe that employers should be obligated to contribute to these benefits just as it is the duty of the employees to contribute their fair share to these plans. The Minister stated in concluding his answer to the question I asked him back on March 9, 1983 that the matter is a complex one and that it also requires the co-operation of the taxpayers to state their entire income. That is not a very fair statement. It seems to me that it is not a complex question. It is a matter of an inequity that is created for one group of our society; a dual standard which is set up by the Government, so it has the best of both worlds. It collects income tax on the increased amount, but will not give the benefits which these employees should receive on the maximum amount. It uses the lesser amount to determine the benefits to these workers.
I ask the Government to take immediate action to overcome this inequity, and to deal with the respective departments. I understand this would include the Department of Revenue and would need to include the Ministers who are responsible for the Canada Pension Plan and for the Unemployment Insurance Commission as well. I believe it is a very simple matter to have rectified, by this Government, in light of the many people who are involved as waiters and waitresses across this country.
There are many single parents who are employees in this profession. There are certainly people on the lower end of the
April 14, 1983

salary scale, and fluctuations in our economy certainly affect those people who work as waiters and waitresses. I ask the Government to take this action at the earliest possible opportunity. It is not complex, as the Minister stated in his answer to my question on March 9, and I would like to know today what action the Government is going to take, and how long it will take for this apparent inequity I have outlined to be rectified.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: INCOME TAX-TREATMENT OF INCOME DERIVED THROUGH SERVICE TIPS. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ACTION
speechtext:
The Hon. Member, as his Party's critic for the Department of National Revenue, should understand the responsibilities of that Department, particularly as they relate to those of other departments. He will be aware, of course, that National Revenue administers the Income Tax Act. I would assume that he does not suggest that the income from tips and gratuities should not be income subject to tax. The Department is carrying out enforcement activity in many areas across the country regarding this type of income because it found that a great deal of it has not been reported. Incidentally, I am not talking here about trifling amounts, but about thousands of dollars of income received over a very few years in this form by certain individuals. I say this because certain media reports have conveyed the assumption that this was a project directed at low income workers.
The question that concerns the Hon. Member is the eligibility of this income under the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Canada Pension Plan. As I understand it, income from tips is regarded as self-employed income and is therefore not insurable earnings under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I also understand that if a person in receipt of tips chooses to do so, he or she could have the income treated as pensionable earnings under the Canada Pension Plan, but would have to pay the higher contribution associated with self-employed income.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) are responsible for the legislation governing the treatment of tips for UIC and CPP purposes. Any changes to the respective acts comes within their purview. The responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue does extend to determining what are insurable or pensionable earnings. These are subject to the provisions of the legislation administered by his colleagues.

SHIPBUILDING-REQUEST FOR ACCELERATION OF VESSEL REPLACEMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at once that I am honoured and flattered that the Minister is here. It shows usual care and attention to procedural matters, particularly where they concern the extended grievances of Members concerning responses they receive to questions they ask, having regard to the shortness of the time and the necessity for brevity, and the difficulty of getting at the heart of the matter in such a short time.
I am here this evening largely because the Minister was quite positive in his response to my question, Mr. Speaker. It had to do with what the Government felt might be desirable
Adjournment Debate
and perhaps possible with respect to bringing on Canadian Government account orders for Canadian shipyards.
As the Minister will be aware, Canadian shipyards provide some 14,000 to 16,000 or 17,000 direct jobs under normal circumstances. He will now be aware that we are down to something of the order of 6,000 or 7,000 jobs, direct and indirect jobs.
That is a little alarming. I hope the Minister can take a minute or two to elaborate, not just on the specific matter I put to him with respect to bringing on a Maritime command fleet replacement program, but also on the requirements of the Department of Oceans and Fisheries for new vessels.
Our Oceanographic Institute at Bedford, one of the most prominent in the world, is now serviced by obsolete ships with obsolete equipment. We have literally hundreds of field programs which must go to sea to be tested and we do not have the vehicles to take them. The potential loss of standing by the Bedford Institute in the world oceanography community disturbs me.
Will the Minister not recognize and address, or at least become an active advocate among his colleagues in the promotion of advancing shipyard orders for fleet replacement programs, first for the navy because we can bring that on now and it will mean thousands of jobs? This would not only mean bringing people back who have been let go, but, perhaps even more important under the circumstances, it will mean the retention of skills and capabilities already there. If we can reach out to the ferries, the coastguard, and the Bedford Institute, which needs a complete fleet replacement program- there is no doubt about that whatsoever-then we would in turn spill benefits back to at least our east coast yards, possibly out to the west coast, with a lot of jobs which will help stabilize one community in the job security area. I am sure this is of interest to the Minister.
I would invite him tonight, in the brief time available to him, to address himself philosophically to whether or not he has been an advocate of early advancement of possible programs, and an advocate of bringing on even earlier mid-term or short-term programs which we know in fact that we do need.
